lieve be tossed out as not.”



“Ah! You make the most of it, I know,” cried Louisa, “but if it were

really so, I should do just the same in her place. If I loved a man, as

she loves the Admiral, I would always be with him, nothing should ever

separate us, and I would rather be overturned by him, than driven

safely by anybody else.”



It was spoken with enthusiasm.



“Had you?” cried he, catching the same tone; “I [[concepts/honour|honour]] you!” And there

was [[motifs/silence|silence]] between them for a little while.



Anne could not immediately fall into a quotation again. The sweet

scenes of [[motifs/autumn|autumn]] were for a while put by, unless some tender [[forms/sonnet|sonnet]],

fraught with the apt analogy of the declining year, with declining

happiness, and the images of youth and [[concepts/hope|hope]], and [[motifs/spring|spring]], all gone

together, blessed her [[motifs/memory|memory]]. She roused herself to say, as they struck

by order into another path, “Is not this one of the ways to Winthrop?”

But nobody heard, or, at least, nobody answered her.



Winthrop, however, or its environs—for young men are, sometimes to be

met with, strolling about near [[motifs/home|home]]—was their destination; and after

another half mile of gradual ascent through large enclosures, where the

ploughs at work, and the fresh made path spoke the farmer counteracting

the sweets of poetical despondence, and meaning to have [[motifs/spring|spring]] again,

they gained the summit of the most considerable [[motifs/hill|hill]], which parted

Uppercross and Winthrop, and soon commanded a full view of the latter,

at the foot of the [[motifs/hill|hill]] on the other side.



Winthrop, without [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] and without dignity, was stretched before

them; an indifferent house, standing low, and hemmed in by the barns

and buildings of a farm-yard.



Mary exclaimed, “Bless me! here is Winthrop. I declare I had no idea!

[[motifs/well|Well]] now, I think we had better turn back; I am excessively tired.”



Henrietta, conscious and ashamed, and seeing no cousin Charles walking

along any path, or leaning against any gate, was ready to do as Mary

wished; but “No!” said Charles Musgrove, and “No, no!” cried Louisa

more eagerly, and taking her sister aside, seemed to be arguing the

matter warmly.



Charles, in the meanwhile, was very decidedly declaring his resolution

of calling on his aunt, now that he was so near; and very evidently,

though more fearfully, trying to induce his wife to go too. But this

was one of the points on which the lady shewed her strength; and when

he recommended the advantage of resting herself a quarter of an hour at

Winthrop, as she felt so tired, she resolutely answered, “Oh! no,

indeed! walking up that [[motifs/hill|hill]] again would do her more harm than any

sitting down could do her good;” and, in short, her look and manner

declared, that go she would not.



After a little succession of these sort of debates and consultations,

it was settled between Charles and his two sisters, that he and

Henrietta should just run down for a few minutes, to see their aunt and

cousins, while the rest of the party waited for them at the top of the

[[motifs/hill|hill]]. Louisa seemed the principal arranger of the plan; and, as she

went a little way with them, down the [[motifs/hill|hill]], still talking to Henrietta,

Mary took the opportunity of looking scornfully around her, and saying

to [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]—



“It is very unpleasant, having such connexions! But, I assure you, I

have never been in the house above twice in my life.”



She received no other answer, than an artificial, assenting smile,

followed by a contemptuous glance, as he turned away, which Anne

perfectly knew the meaning of.



The brow of the [[motifs/hill|hill]], where they remained, was a cheerful spot: Louisa

returned; and Mary, finding a comfortable seat for herself on the step

of a stile, was very [[motifs/well|well]] satisfied so long as the others all stood

about her; but when Louisa drew [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] away, to try for a

gleaning of nuts in an adjoining hedge-row, and they were gone by

degrees quite out of sight and sound, Mary was happy no longer; she

quarrelled with her own seat, was sure Louisa had got a much better

somewhere, and nothing could prevent her from going to look for a

better also. She turned through the same gate, but could not see them.

Anne found a nice seat for her, on a dry sunny bank, under the

hedge-row, in which she had no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of their still being, in some spot

or other. Mary sat down for a moment, but it would not do; she was sure

Louisa had found a better seat somewhere else, and she would go on till

she overtook her.



Anne, really tired herself, was glad to sit down; and she very soon

heard [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] and Louisa in the hedge-row, behind her, as if

making their way back along the rough, wild sort of channel, down the

centre. They were speaking as they drew near. Louisa’s voice was the

first distinguished. She seemed to be in the middle of some eager

speech. What Anne first heard was—



“And so, I made her go. I could not bear that she should be frightened

from the visit by such nonsense. What! would I be turned back from

doing a thing that I had determined to do, and that I knew to be right,

by the airs and interference of such a person, or of any person I may

say? No, I have no idea of being so easily persuaded. When I have made

up my mind, I have made it; and Henrietta seemed entirely to have made

up hers to call at Winthrop to-day; and yet, she was as near giving it

up, out of nonsensical complaisance!”



“She would have turned back then, but for you?”



“She would indeed. I am almost ashamed to say it.”



“Happy for her, to have such a mind as yours at hand! After the hints

you gave just now, which did but confirm my own observations, the last

[[motifs/time|time]] I was in company with him, I need not affect to have no

comprehension of what is going on. I see that more than a mere dutiful

morning visit to your aunt was in question; and woe betide him, and her


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Non essere mai scartato come inutile.”



“Ah! Ne approfitti al massimo, lo so,” esclamò Louisa, “ma se fosse…”

“Davvero… anch’io farei lo stesso al suo posto. Se amassi un uomo, come…”

Lei ama l’ammiraglio… Io sarei sempre con lui… Niente mai dovrebbe separarci…

Separatemi da lui… Preferirei essere rovesciata da lui, piuttosto che essere allontanata da lui.

“Al sicuro da chiunque altro.”



Fu detto con entusiasmo.



“L’hai avuta?” gridò lui, usando lo stesso tono; “Ti rispetto davvero!” E così.

Per un po’ regnò il [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] tra di loro.



Non riuscì subito a ricadere nella solita routine delle citazioni… La dolcezza…

Le scene d’[[motifs/autumn|autunno]] furono per un po’ messe da parte, a meno che non comparisse qualche tenero [[forms/sonnet|sonetto]].

Titolo:  
Carico dell’appropriata metafora dell’anno che declina…

La felicità, le immagini della giovinezza e della [[concepts/hope|>speranza]], e la [[motifs/spring|Primavera]], tutto scomparso.

Insieme, lodarono la sua [[motifs/memory|memoria]]. Si svegliò e disse, mentre loro suonavano.

“Indirizzandolo verso un altro percorso… Non è forse questa una delle strade che portano a Winthrop?”

Ma nessuno la sentì, o almeno, nessuno le rispose.



Winthrop, però… o i suoi dintorni: perché, a volte, è proprio così che sono i giovani uomini.

Incontrarsi, passeggiare nei dintorni di [[motifs/home|>casa]], era il loro destinazione; e dopo.

Un’altra mezza miglia di salita graduale attraverso ampi recinti…

“La terra arata sotto il sole: la nuova strada appena tracciata testimonia il lavoro del contadino”.

I piaceri di quella malinconia poetica, e la speranza di poter rivivere ancora una volta.

Raggiunsero la cima della più imponente [[motifs/hill|collina]], che si separava in due parti.

Uppercross e Winthrop… e presto si poté ammirare completamente quest’ultimo.

Ai piedi della [[motifs/hill|collina]], dall'altra parte.



Winthrop, privo di [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e di dignità, fu disteso davanti a.

Loro; una casa indifferente, situata in basso e circondata dai granai.

e gli edifici di un cortile agricolo.



Mary esclamò: “Mio Dio! Ecco qui Winthrop. Devo ammettere che non ne avevo la minima idea!”

Beh, ora penso che sia meglio tornare indietro; sono estremamente stanco.



Henrietta, consapevole e imbarazzata, non vedeva da nessuna parte il cugino Charles…

“Ogni percorso, o qualsiasi cancello su cui appoggiarsi… era pronto ad agire come fece Mary.”

Volevano farlo; ma “No!”, disse Charles Musgrove, e “No, no!”, gridò Louisa.

Con maggiore impazienza, portò sua sorella da parte e sembrava discutere con lei…

Si trattava di qualcosa di davvero caloroso.



Nel frattempo, Charles dichiarava con fermezza la sua determinazione.

Di andare a trovare sua zia, ora che era così vicino… e ovviamente,

Con più timore, cercò di convincere anche sua moglie ad andare con lui… Ma questo…

Fu uno degli argomenti su cui la signora dimostrò la sua forza; e quando…

Consigliò l’importanza di riposarsi per un quarto d’ora…

“Winthrop… poiché si sentiva così stanca, rispose con decisione: ‘Oh, no…’”

Davvero! Risalire di nuovo quella [[motifs/hill|collina]] le farebbe più male di qualsiasi altra cosa.

“Risiedersi un po’ le farebbe bene…”, insomma, il suo aspetto e il suo comportamento indicavano chiaramente questo.

Disse chiaramente che non avrebbe andato.



Dopo una serie di dibattiti e consultazioni di questo tipo…

Fu concordato tra Charles e le sue due sorelle che lui…

Henrietta dovrebbe semplicemente correre giù per qualche minuto, per incontrare sua zia…

Cugini… mentre il resto del gruppo li aspettava in cima alla…

[[motifs/hill|collina]]. Sembra che Louisa fosse la principale organizzatrice del piano; e, dato che.

Andò un po’ più in là con loro, giù per la [[motifs/hill|collina]], continuando a parlare con Henrietta.

Mary approfittò dell’occasione per guardarsi intorno con disprezzo e disse…

A [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]].



“È davvero sgradevole avere simili legami… Ma vi assicuro che…”

Nella mia vita non sono mai stato due volte nella casa sopra.



Non ricevette alcuna altra risposta, solo un sorriso artificioso e di consenso.

Con uno sguardo di disprezzo, si allontanò, e Anne…

Conosceva perfettamente il significato di quella parola.



La cima della [[motifs/hill|collina]], dove si trovavano, era un luogo piacevole: Louisa

“Tornato indietro; e Mary si trovò un posto comodo sul gradino…”

Di quel certo stile, era molto [[motifs/well|soddisfatto]] finché tutti gli altri rimanevano al suo fianco.

Parlava di lei; ma quando Louisa portò via [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] per provare a.

Raccogliere noci lungo la siepe adiacente… e poi se ne sono andati.

Lontana da ogni vista e suono, Mary non era più felice…

Si scontrò con il proprio posto… Era sicura che Louisa ne avesse trovato uno molto migliore.

Da qualche parte… e nulla poteva impedirle di andare a cercarla.

Anche meglio così. Entrò dallo stesso cancello, ma non riuscì a vederli.

Un posto tranquillo e soleggiato

Quel filare di alberi, nel quale non aveva alcun [[concepts/doubt|>dubbio]] che fossero ancora lì, da qualche parte.

O altro ancora… Mary si sedette per un momento, ma non andava bene: ne era sicura.

Louisa aveva trovato un posto migliore da qualche altra parte e avrebbe continuato lì.

Lei la superò.



Anne, davvero stanca, fu felice di potersi sedere; e presto…

Sentì [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] e Louisa nella siepe, dietro di lei, come se.

Ritornando lungo quel canale ruvido e selvaggio…

Centro… Parlavano mentre si avvicinavano. La voce di Louisa era…

Per la prima volta distinta… Sembrava essere al centro di un’atmosfera di grande entusiasmo.

Parola… Quello che Anne sentì per prima cosa fu…



“E così, la costrinsi ad andarsene. Non potevo sopportare l’idea che potesse avere paura.”

Da una visita piena di assurdità… Che cosa? Mi verrebbero negati i diritti che mi spettano?

Fare ciò che avevo deciso di fare, e sapevo essere la cosa giusta.

Titolo:  
A causa delle pretese e degli interventi di una persona del genere, o di qualsiasi altra persona…

Mai dire mai…

Deciso… e sembra che anche Henrietta abbia preso la sua decisione.

Oggi poteva chiamare Winthrop… eppure, era quasi sul punto di farlo.

“Su, via da questa insensata compiacenza!”



Se non fosse stato per te, lei si sarebbe girata indietro in quel momento…



“Lo avrebbe davvero fatto… Mi vergogno quasi di dirlo.”



“Felice per lei, avere a disposizione una mente come la tua… Dopo tutti quei suggerimenti…”

Il titolo che avete appena menzionato conferma soltanto le mie osservazioni… l’ultima in particolare.

Durante quella [[motifs/time|periode]], ero in sua compagnia; non c’è bisogno che finga di non averla conosciuta.

Comprendere ciò che sta accadendo… È qualcosa di molto più profondo di un semplice dovere.

La visita mattutina alla zia era in discussione… E ahimè, per lui e per lei.

too, when it comes to things of consequence, when they are placed in

circumstances requiring fortitude and strength of mind, if she have not

resolution enough to resist idle interference in such a trifle as this.

Your sister is an amiable creature; but _yours_ is the character of

decision and firmness, I see. If you value her conduct or happiness,

infuse as much of your own spirit into her as you can. But this, no

[[concepts/doubt|doubt]], you have been always doing. It is the worst evil of too yielding

and indecisive a character, that no influence over it can be depended

on. You are never sure of a good impression being durable; everybody

may sway it. Let those who would be happy be firm. Here is a nut,” said

he, catching one down from an upper bough, “to exemplify: a beautiful

glossy nut, which, blessed with original strength, has outlived all the

storms of [[motifs/autumn|autumn]]. Not a puncture, not a weak spot anywhere. This nut,”

he continued, with playful solemnity, “while so many of his brethren

have fallen and been trodden under foot, is still in possession of all

the happiness that a hazel nut can be supposed capable of.” Then

returning to his former earnest tone—“My first wish for all whom I am

interested in, is that they should be firm. If Louisa Musgrove would be

beautiful and happy in her November of life, she will cherish all her

present powers of mind.”



He had done, and was unanswered. It would have surprised Anne if Louisa

could have readily answered such a speech: words of such interest,

spoken with such serious warmth! She could imagine what Louisa was

feeling. For herself, she feared to move, lest she should be seen.

While she remained, a bush of low rambling holly protected her, and

they were moving on. Before they were beyond her hearing, however,

Louisa spoke again.



“Mary is good-natured enough in many respects,” said she; “but she does

sometimes provoke me excessively, by her nonsense and [[concepts/pride|pride]]—the Elliot

[[concepts/pride|pride]]. She has a great deal too much of the Elliot [[concepts/pride|pride]]. We do so wish

that Charles had married Anne instead. I suppose you know he wanted to

marry Anne?”



After a moment’s pause, [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] said—



“Do you mean that she refused him?”



“Oh! yes; certainly.”



“When did that happen?”



“I do not exactly know, for Henrietta and I were at school at the [[motifs/time|time]];

but I believe about a year before he married Mary. I wish she had

accepted him. We should all have liked her a great deal better; and

papa and mamma always think it was her great friend [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]’s

doing, that she did not. They think Charles might not be learned and

bookish enough to please [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]], and that therefore, she

persuaded Anne to refuse him.”



The sounds were retreating, and Anne distinguished no more. Her own

emotions still kept her fixed. She had much to recover from, before she

could move. The listener’s proverbial fate was not absolutely hers; she

had heard no evil of herself, but she had heard a great deal of very

painful import. She saw how her own character was considered by Captain

Wentworth, and there had been just that degree of feeling and curiosity

about her in his manner which must give her extreme agitation.



As soon as she could, she went after Mary, and having found, and walked

back with her to their former station, by the stile, felt some comfort

in their whole party being immediately afterwards collected, and once

more in motion together. Her spirits wanted the [[concepts/solitude|solitude]] and [[motifs/silence|silence]]

which only numbers could give.



Charles and Henrietta returned, bringing, as may be conjectured,

Charles Hayter with them. The minutiae of the business Anne could not

attempt to understand; even [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] did not seem admitted to

perfect confidence here; but that there had been a withdrawing on the

gentleman’s side, and a relenting on the lady’s, and that they were now

very glad to be together again, did not admit a [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]. Henrietta looked

a little ashamed, but very [[motifs/well|well]] pleased;—Charles Hayter exceedingly

happy: and they were devoted to each other almost from the first

instant of their all setting forward for Uppercross.



Everything now marked out Louisa for [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]; nothing could

be plainer; and where many divisions were necessary, or even where they

were not, they walked side by side nearly as much as the other two. In

a long strip of meadow land, where there was ample space for all, they

were thus divided, forming three distinct parties; and to that party of

the three which boasted least animation, and least complaisance, Anne

necessarily belonged. She joined Charles and Mary, and was tired enough

to be very glad of Charles’s other arm; but Charles, though in very

good humour with her, was out of temper with his wife. Mary had shewn

herself disobliging to him, and was now to reap the consequence, which

consequence was his dropping her arm almost every moment to cut off the

heads of some nettles in the hedge with his switch; and when Mary began

to complain of it, and lament her being ill-used, according to custom,

in being on the hedge side, while Anne was never incommoded on the

other, he dropped the arms of both to hunt after a weasel which he had

a momentary glance of, and they could hardly get him along at all.



This long meadow bordered a lane, which their footpath, at the end of

it was to [[motifs/cross|cross]], and when the party had all reached the gate of exit,

the carriage advancing in the same direction, which had been some [[motifs/time|time]]

heard, was just coming up, and proved to be [[characters/admiral-croft|Admiral Croft]]’s gig. He and

his wife had taken their intended drive, and were returning [[motifs/home|home]]. Upon

hearing how long a walk the young people had engaged in, they kindly

offered a seat to any lady who might be particularly tired; it would

save her a full mile, and they were going through Uppercross. The

Altro… Lasciò cadere entrambe le braccia e iniziò a inseguire una donnola che aveva…

Con uno sguardo fugace, riuscivano a malapena a farlo procedere.



Questo lungo prato era delimitato da un sentiero; alla fine di esso…

Era il momento di [[motifs/cross|attraversare]]; quando tutti i partecipanti furono arrivati alla porta d’uscita.

Il carrozza procedeva nella stessa direzione; era già trascorso un po’ di tempo.

Avevano appena sentito parlare di lui; stava per arrivare e si rivelò essere la nave gigante dell’[[characters/admiral-croft|Ammiraglio Croft]]. Lui e.

Sua moglie aveva fatto il viaggio che avevano pianificato e stavano tornando a [[motifs/home|>casa]]. Mentre.

Dopo aver saputo quanto tempo avevano camminato i giovani, si mostrarono gentili…

Offriva un posto a qualsiasi signora che potesse sentirsi particolarmente stanca; lo faceva volentieri.

salvarla per un intero miglio… e stavano attraversando Uppercross.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_10--part_04" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 10 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 10" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/home,motif/horse,motif/pain,motif/time,motif/well,concept/friendship,concept/pride,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


invitation was general, and generally declined. The Miss Musgroves were

not at all tired, and Mary was either offended, by not being asked

before any of the others, or what Louisa called the Elliot [[concepts/pride|pride]] could

not endure to make a third in a one [[motifs/horse|horse]] chaise.



The walking party had crossed the lane, and were surmounting an

opposite stile, and the Admiral was putting his [[motifs/horse|horse]] in motion again,

when [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] cleared the hedge in a moment to say something

to his sister. The something might be guessed by its effects.



“Miss Elliot, I am sure _you_ are tired,” cried Mrs Croft. “Do let us

have the pleasure of taking you [[motifs/home|home]]. Here is excellent room for three,

I assure you. If we were all like you, I believe we might sit four. You

must, indeed, you must.”



Anne was still in the lane; and though instinctively beginning to

decline, she was not allowed to proceed. The Admiral’s kind urgency

came in support of his wife’s; they would not be refused; they

compressed themselves into the smallest possible space to leave her a

corner, and [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], without saying a word, turned to her,

and quietly obliged her to be assisted into the carriage.



Yes; he had done it. She was in the carriage, and felt that he had

placed her there, that his will and his hands had done it, that she

owed it to his perception of her fatigue, and his resolution to give

her rest. She was very much affected by the view of his disposition

towards her, which all these things made apparent. This little

circumstance seemed the completion of all that had gone before. She

understood him. He could not forgive her, but he could not be

unfeeling. Though condemning her for the past, and considering it with

high and unjust resentment, though perfectly careless of her, and

though becoming attached to another, still he could not see her suffer,

without the [[motifs/desire|desire]] of giving her relief. It was a remainder of former

sentiment; it was an impulse of pure, though unacknowledged [[concepts/friendship|friendship]];

it was a proof of his own warm and amiable heart, which she could not

contemplate without emotions so compounded of pleasure and [[motifs/pain|pain]], that

she knew not which prevailed.



Her answers to the kindness and the remarks of her companions were at

first unconsciously given. They had travelled half their way along the

rough lane, before she was quite awake to what they said. She then

found them talking of “Frederick.”



“He certainly means to have one or other of those two girls, Sophy,”

said the Admiral; “but there is no saying which. He has been running

after them, too, long enough, one would think, to make up his mind. Ay,

this comes of the peace. If it were war now, he would have settled it

long ago. We sailors, Miss Elliot, cannot afford to make long

courtships in [[motifs/time|time]] of war. How many days was it, my dear, between the

first [[motifs/time|time]] of my seeing you and our sitting down together in our

lodgings at North Yarmouth?”



“We had better not talk about it, my dear,” replied Mrs Croft,

pleasantly; “for if Miss Elliot were to hear how soon we came to an

understanding, she would never be persuaded that we could be happy

together. I had known you by character, however, long before.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], and I had heard of you as a very pretty girl, and what were we

to wait for besides? I do not like having such things so long in hand.

I wish Frederick would spread a little more canvass, and bring us [[motifs/home|home]]

one of these young ladies to Kellynch. Then there would always be

company for them. And very nice young ladies they both are; I hardly

know one from the other.”



“Very good humoured, unaffected girls, indeed,” said Mrs Croft, in a

tone of calmer praise, such as made Anne suspect that her keener powers

might not consider either of them as quite worthy of her brother; “and

a very respectable family. One could not be connected with better

people. My dear Admiral, that post! we shall certainly take that post.”



But by coolly giving the reins a better direction herself they happily

passed the danger; and by once afterwards judiciously putting out her

hand they neither fell into a rut, nor ran foul of a dung-cart; and

Anne, with some amusement at their style of driving, which she imagined

no bad representation of the general guidance of their affairs, found

herself safely deposited by them at the Cottage.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

L’invito era aperto a tutti, ma fu in generale rifiutato. Le signorine Musgrove…

Affatto stanco… e Mary, probabilmente offesa dal fatto che non le fosse stato chiesto nulla.

Prima che chiunque altro potesse farlo, o prima che ciò che Louisa definiva l’[[concepts/pride|orgoglio]] della famiglia Elliot avvenisse.

Non si poteva sopportare l’idea di dover fare il terzo in una carrozza a un solo cavallo.



La compagnia di viaggiatori aveva attraversato la strada e stava iniziando ad ascendere…

Stile completamente opposto; l’ammiraglio stava di nuovo facendo muovere il suo [[motifs/horse|cavallo]].

quando [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] superò rapidamente la siepe per dire qualcosa

A sua sorella. Quell’“qualcosa” può essere intuito dai suoi effetti.



“Signorina Elliot, sono sicura che lei sia stanca”, esclamò la signora Croft. “Lasci che l’aiutiamo…”

Ho il piacere di accompagnarvi a [[motifs/home|>casa]]. Ecco una stanza eccellente per tre persone.

“Ve lo assicuro: se fossimo tutti come voi, credo che potremmo starci in quattro.”

“Devi proprio farlo, assolutamente.”



Anne era ancora nel sentiero; e sebbene istintivamente avesse già iniziato…

Declino: Non le fu permesso di procedere. L’urgenza gentile dell’ammiraglio

“Arrivarono in sostegno di sua moglie; non avrebbero ricevuto rifiuti; loro…”

Si sono compressi nello spazio più piccolo possibile per lasciarle posto.

All’angolo, e [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]], senza dire una parola, si girò verso di lei.

E in silenzio la aiutò a salire nella carrozza.



Sì; l’aveva fatto. Lei era nella carrozza e sentiva che lui l’aveva fatto.

La posero lì, perché era stata la sua volontà e le sue mani a farlo… Lei…

Il titolo si basa sulla sua percezione della stanchezza di lei e sulla sua determinazione ad aiutarla.

Il resto della sua vita… Fu profondamente influenzata dal modo in cui lui si comportava.

Verso di lei, e tutto ciò rendeva evidente questo legame… Questa piccola…

La circostanza sembrava rappresentare la conclusione di tutto ciò che era accaduto prima. Lei…

Lo capiva… Non riusciva a perdonarla, ma non poteva nemmeno…

Senza cuore. Anche se la condanna per il passato e la considera in questo modo…

Amarezza profonda e ingiusta, nonostante lui fosse totalmente indifferente verso di lei…

Anche se si era legato a un’altra persona, non riusciva comunque a sopportare di vederla soffrire.

Senza il [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di alleviarla. Era solo un residuo del passato.

Sentimento. Era un impulso di pura, sebbene non riconosciuta, [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]].

Era una prova del suo cuore caldo e affabile, qualcosa che lei non poteva ignorare.

Ammirarlo senza emozioni, un misto di piacere e [[motifs/pain|dolore]], in modo tale che.

Non sapeva quale dei due sentimenti prevalesse.



Le sue risposte alla gentilezza e ai commenti dei suoi compagni erano…

Primo dono ricevuto inconsciamente… Avevano percorso già metà del cammino…

“Una strada accidentata… Prima ancora di rendersi completamente conto di ciò che stavano dicendo.”

Li ho trovati che parlavano di “Frederick”.



“Di certo intende prendersi una di quelle due ragazze, Sophy.”

Disse l’ammiraglio: “Ma non si può dire con certezza… Lui continua a muoversi, senza una direzione precisa”.

Dopo di loro, anche… abbastanza tempo, si direbbe, per prendere una decisione. Ah…

Questo è il risultato della pace… Se ora ci fosse la guerra, l’avrebbe già risolta.

Molto tempo fa… Noi marinai, signorina Elliot, non potevamo permetterci di viaggiare per lunghi periodi.

Le corteggiature in tempi di guerra. Quanti giorni sono trascorsi, mio caro, tra.

La prima volta che ti ho visto e che ci siamo seduti insieme.

“Alloggi a North Yarmouth?”



“Meglio non parlarne, caro mio”, rispose la signora Croft.

“Piacerevolmente… perché se la signorina Elliot dovesse sentire quanto in fretta siamo arrivati…”

Conoscendo la situazione, non sarebbe mai stata convinta che potessimo essere felici.

“Fin da prima conoscevo il tuo carattere…”



“Beh, avevo sentito dire che fossi una ragazza molto bella. E poi, cosa stavamo facendo?”

Aspettare oltre a questo? Non mi piace tenere queste cose per troppo tempo a mia disposizione.

Vorrei che Frederick distribuisse un po’ più di volantini e ci portasse [[motifs/home|a casa]].

Una di queste giovani signore andrebbe a Kellynch… Allora ci sarebbe sempre qualcuno.

“Una compagnia perfetta per loro… Sono entrambe giovani donne molto carine; a malapena…”

“Non si riesce a distinguere l’uno dall’altro.”



“Ragazze davvero di buon umore e senza affettazioni”, disse la signora Croft.

Titolo:  
Un tono di lode più misurato… che fece sospettare ad Anne che le sue capacità fossero davvero più acute del solito.

“Potrebbe non ritenere nessuno dei due davvero degno di suo fratello; ‘e’…”

Una famiglia davvero rispettabile… Non si potrebbe desiderare legami migliori di questi.

“Gente… Mio caro Ammiraglio, quel posto! Sicuramente lo prenderemo.”



Ma prendendo lei stessa le redini e guidandole nella giusta direzione, tutto andò felicemente per il meglio.

Superata la pericolosa situazione, in seguito agì con saggezza…

Non caddero mai in una routine né si scontrarono con un carretto pieno di letame…

Anne, con un certo divertimento per il loro stile di guida…

Nessuna cattiva rappresentazione delle linee guida generali per la gestione dei loro affari

Essa stessa fu depositata al sicuro da loro nella Casetta.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11--part_01" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 11 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 11" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/hill,motif/memory,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/noon,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/water,motif/winter,concept/friendship,concept/nature,concept/self,character/captain_wentworth,character/lady_russell"></span>


CHAPTER XI.





The [[motifs/time|time]] now approached for [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]’s return: the day was even

fixed; and Anne, being engaged to join her as soon as she was

resettled, was looking forward to an early removal to Kellynch, and

beginning to think how her own comfort was likely to be affected by it.



It would place her in the same village with [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], within

half a mile of him; they would have to frequent the same church, and

there must be intercourse between the two families. This was against

her; but on the other hand, he spent so much of his [[motifs/time|time]] at Uppercross,

that in removing thence she might be considered rather as leaving him

behind, than as going towards him; and, upon the whole, she believed

she must, on this interesting question, be the gainer, almost as

certainly as in her change of domestic society, in leaving poor Mary

for [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]].



She wished it might be possible for her to avoid ever seeing Captain

Wentworth at the Hall: those rooms had witnessed former meetings which

would be brought too painfully before her; but she was yet more anxious

for the possibility of [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] and [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] never meeting

anywhere. They did not like each other, and no renewal of acquaintance

now could do any good; and were [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] to see them together, she

might think that he had too much [[concepts/self|self]]-possession, and she too little.



These points formed her chief solicitude in anticipating her removal

from Uppercross, where she felt she had been stationed quite long

enough. Her usefulness to little Charles would always give some

sweetness to the [[motifs/memory|memory]] of her two months’ visit there, but he was

gaining strength apace, and she had nothing else to stay for.



The conclusion of her visit, however, was diversified in a way which

she had not at all imagined. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], after being unseen and

unheard of at Uppercross for two whole days, appeared again among them

to justify himself by a relation of what had kept him away.



A letter from his friend, Captain Harville, having found him out at

last, had brought intelligence of Captain Harville’s being settled with

his family at Lyme for the [[motifs/winter|winter]]; of their being therefore, quite

unknowingly, within twenty miles of each other. Captain Harville had

never been in good health since a severe wound which he received two

years before, and [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s anxiety to see him had determined

him to go immediately to Lyme. He had been there for four-and-twenty

hours. His acquittal was complete, his [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] warmly honoured, a

lively interest excited for his friend, and his description of the fine

country about Lyme so feelingly attended to by the party, that an

earnest [[motifs/desire|desire]] to see Lyme themselves, and a project for going thither

was the consequence.



The young people were all wild to see Lyme. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] talked of

going there again himself, it was only seventeen miles from Uppercross;

though November, the weather was by no means bad; and, in short,

Louisa, who was the most eager of the eager, having formed the

resolution to go, and besides the pleasure of doing as she liked, being

now armed with the idea of merit in maintaining her own way, bore down

all the wishes of her father and mother for putting it off till [[motifs/summer|summer]];

and to Lyme they were to go—Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]].



The first heedless scheme had been to go in the morning and return at

[[motifs/night|night]]; but to this Mr Musgrove, for the sake of his horses, would not

consent; and when it came to be rationally considered, a day in the

middle of November would not leave much [[motifs/time|time]] for seeing a new place,

after deducting seven hours, as the [[concepts/nature|nature]] of the country required, for

going and returning. They were, consequently, to stay the [[motifs/night|night]] there,

and not to be expected back till the next day’s dinner. This was felt

to be a considerable amendment; and though they all met at the Great

House at rather an early breakfast hour, and set off very punctually,

it was so much past [[motifs/noon|noon]] before the two carriages, Mr Musgrove’s coach

containing the four ladies, and Charles’s curricle, in which he drove

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], were descending the long [[motifs/hill|hill]] into Lyme, and

entering upon the still steeper street of the town itself, that it was

very evident they would not have more than [[motifs/time|time]] for looking about them,

before the light and warmth of the day were gone.



After securing accommodations, and ordering a dinner at one of the

inns, the next thing to be done was unquestionably to walk directly

down to the sea. They were come too late in the year for any amusement

or variety which Lyme, as a public place, might offer. The rooms were

shut up, the lodgers almost all gone, scarcely any family but of the

residents left; and, as there is nothing to admire in the buildings

themselves, the remarkable situation of the town, the principal street

almost hurrying into the [[motifs/water|water]], the walk to the Cobb, skirting round

the pleasant little bay, which, in the season, is animated with bathing

machines and company; the Cobb itself, its old wonders and new

improvements, with the very beautiful line of cliffs stretching out to

the east of the town, are what the stranger’s eye will seek; and a very

strange stranger it must be, who does not see charms in the immediate

environs of Lyme, to make him wish to know it better. The scenes in its

neighbourhood, Charmouth, with its high grounds and extensive sweeps of

country, and still more, its sweet, retired bay, backed by dark cliffs,

where fragments of low rock among the sands, make it the happiest spot

for watching the flow of the tide, for sitting in unwearied

contemplation; the woody varieties of the cheerful village of Up Lyme;

and, above all, Pinny, with its green chasms between romantic rocks,


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XI.





Il momento del ritorno di [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] si avvicinava; era anche una giornata serena.

Titolo:  
Fissa… e Anne, che avrebbe dovuto raggiungerla non appena fosse stata pronta…

Risiedutosi in un nuovo luogo, aspettava con impazienza di trasferirsi presto a Kellynch.

Iniziò a chiedersi in che modo il proprio comfort potesse essere influenzato da quella situazione.



Ciò la metterebbe nello stesso villaggio di [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]], all’interno.

Mezzo miglio di distanza… Avrebbero dovuto frequentare la stessa chiesa…

Deve esserci un rapporto tra le due famiglie. Questo era contrario…

Lei; ma d'altra parte, trascorreva così tanto del suo [[motifs/time|tempo]] a Uppercross.

Titolo:  
Tale da poter essere considerata, nel allontanarsi da lì, come se lo stesse lasciando.

Dietro di lui, piuttosto che dirigersi verso di lui… E, in generale, lei credeva…

In questa interessante questione, lei deve sicuramente essere la vincitrice… quasi certamente.

Certamente, come nel suo cambiamento di ambiente domestico, abbandonando la povera Mary…

Per [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]].



Vorrebbe tanto poter evitare di incontrare mai più il Capitano…

Wentworth alla Hall: quelle stanze avevano assistito a incontri passati…

Una verità troppo dolorosa da affrontare… ma la sua ansia aumentava ancora di più.

per la possibilità che [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] e [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] non si incontrassero mai

In nessun luogo. Non si piacevano affatto, e non c’era alcuna possibilità di rinnovare quella conoscenza.

Ora non avrebbero potuto fare alcun bene; e se [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] li vedesse insieme.

Si potrebbe pensare che lui abbia troppa [[concepts/self|autocontrollo]], mentre lei ne abbia troppo poco.



Questi aspetti rappresentavano la sua principale preoccupazione riguardo al suo possibile trasferimento.

Da Uppercross, dove sentiva di essere rimasta da un bel po’…

Basta. Il suo valore per il piccolo Charles sarebbe sempre stato significativo…

Una dolcezza nella [[motifs/memory|ricordo]] della sua visita di due mesi lì, ma lui.

Acquistando rapidamente forza, non le restava più nulla per cui rimanere.



Tuttavia, la conclusione della sua visita si rivelò diversificata in modo tale che…

Non se l'era affatto immaginata. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]], dopo essere rimasto nascosto e.

Per due interi giorni non si sentì parlare di lui a Uppercross… Poi ricomparve tra loro.

Per giustificarsi, raccontò cosa lo aveva trattenuto lontano.



Titolo:  
Una lettera dal suo amico, il Capitano Harville, che lo ha scoperto…

Ultimamente, era arrivata la notizia che il Capitano Harville si fosse sistemato in un luogo stabile.

La sua famiglia trascorreva l[[motifs/winter|inverno]] a Lyme; pertanto, erano completamente.

Senza saperlo, a meno di venti miglia l’uno dall’altro… Il Capitano Harville aveva…

Da quando ha riportato una grave ferita, non è mai stato in buona salute…

Anni prima, l’ansia di [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] di rivederlo aveva preso il sopravvento.

Mandarlo immediatamente a Lyme. Era stato lì per ventiquattro ore.

Ore. La sua assoluzione fu completa; la sua [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]] fu rispettata con calore.

Un vivo interesse si destò per il suo amico, e la sua descrizione di ciò che era bello…

Un paese che si prende cura con tanta attenzione di Lyme…

Un sincero [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di vedere personalmente Lyme, e un progetto per recarsi laggiù.

Fu la conseguenza di ciò.



I giovani erano tutti entusiasti di vedere Lyme. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] ne parlava con grande interesse.

“Ci va di nuovo lui stesso… Dista soltanto diciassette miglia da Uppercross…”

Nonostante fosse novembre, il tempo non era affatto cattivo; insomma…

Louisa, la più desiderosa di tutte, aveva già deciso…

La determinazione di partire… e, oltre al piacere di fare ciò che desiderava, c’era anche…

Ora armata dell’idea che il merito sia fondamentale per perseguire la propria strada, procedette con determinazione.

A tutti i desideri di suo padre e sua madre di rimandare la cosa fino all’[[motifs/summer|estate]];

E verso Lyme avrebbero dovuto recarsi: Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa… e altri ancora.

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]].



Il primo piano imprudente consisteva nel partire al mattino e tornare…

Di [[motifs/night|notte]];] ma per quanto riguarda questo signor Musgrove, per amore dei suoi cavalli, non lo avrebbe fatto.

Consenso; e quando si considera la cosa razionalmente, un giorno trascorso…

A metà di novembre non restava molto [[motifs/time|tempo]] per visitare un posto nuovo.

Dopo aver detratto sette ore, come richiesto dalla [[concepts/nature|>natura]] del paese, per.

Andando e tornando indietro, di conseguenza avrebbero trascorso la [[motifs/night|notte]] lì.

E non si prevedeva che tornasse prima della cena del giorno seguente… Questo fu ciò che tutti pensarono.

Un emendamento considerevole… E sebbene si incontrassero tutti al Grande…

House si alzò molto presto per colazione e partì puntualmente.

Erano passate molte ore dopo [[motifs/noon|mattina]] quando arrivarono i due vagoni, il vagone di Mr Musgrove.

Il calesse di Charles, con le quattro signore a bordo

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] stava scendendo la lunga [[motifs/hill|collina]] verso Lyme, e.

Entrando nella strada ancora più ripida del centro della città…

Era molto evidente che non avrebbero avuto più di [[motifs/time|tempo]] per guardarsi intorno.

prima che la luce e il calore del giorno svanissero.



Dopo essersi sistemato e aver ordinato la cena in uno dei…

Titolo:  
Dopo le locande, l’azione successiva da intraprendere era senza dubbio quella di andare direttamente…

Verso il mare… Erano arrivati troppo tardi nell’anno per potersi divertire in alcun modo.

Le varietà che Lyme, in quanto luogo pubblico, poteva offrire… Le stanze erano…

Zitti, gli inquilini se ne sono andati quasi tutti… Non ci sono più famiglie, tranne quella…

I residenti se ne erano andati; e, poiché non c’era nulla di degno di ammirazione nelle costruzioni…

La strada principale della città e la sua situazione particolare

Quasi correndo verso l’[[motifs/water|acqua]], il cammino verso il Cobb, aggirando intorno.

La deliziosa piccola baia, che durante la stagione si anima con le persone che vanno a fare il bagno.

Macchine e compagnia: il Cobb stesso, le sue antiche meraviglie e quelle nuove

Miglioramenti… con quella meravigliosa linea di scogliere che si estende all’infinito

A est della città ci sono quelle cose che lo sguardo di uno straniero cercherà sicuramente… e molto altro ancora.

“Che strano individuo deve essere chi non riesce a scorgere le attrazioni presenti nelle cose immediatamente davanti a sé…”

I dintorni di Lyme, che spingono a volerli conoscere meglio. Le scene che si svolgono in quel luogo…

Quartiere di Charmouth, con le sue alture e i suoi ampi panorami

Paese… e soprattutto la sua dolce baia, riparata da scogli scuri.

Dove i frammenti di roccia si mescolano alla sabbia, creando il luogo più felice

Per osservare il flusso della marea, per restare seduti senza stancarsi…

Contemplazione: le varietà arboree del sereno villaggio di Up Lyme

E, soprattutto, Pinny, con le sue voragini verdi tra rocce dal fascino romantico…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11--part_02" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 11 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 11" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,motif/winter,concept/friendship,concept/history,concept/melancholy,form/history,character/captain_benwick,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


where the scattered forest trees and orchards of luxuriant growth,

declare that many a generation must have passed away since the first

partial falling of the cliff prepared the ground for such a state,

where a scene so wonderful and so lovely is exhibited, as may more than

equal any of the resembling scenes of the far-famed Isle of Wight:

these places must be visited, and visited again, to make the worth of

Lyme understood.



The party from Uppercross passing down by the now deserted and

[[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] looking rooms, and still descending, soon found themselves

on the sea-shore; and lingering only, as all must linger and gaze on a

first return to the sea, who ever deserved to look on it at all,

proceeded towards the Cobb, equally their object in itself and on

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s account: for in a small house, near the foot of an

old pier of unknown date, were the Harvilles settled. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]

turned in to call on his friend; the others walked on, and he was to

join them on the Cobb.



They were by no means tired of wondering and admiring; and not even

Louisa seemed to feel that they had parted with [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] long,

when they saw him coming after them, with three companions, all [[motifs/well|well]]

known already, by description, to be Captain and Mrs Harville, and a

[[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]], who was staying with them.



[[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] had some [[motifs/time|time]] ago been first lieutenant of the Laconia;

and the account which [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] had given of him, on his return

from Lyme before, his warm praise of him as an excellent young man and

an officer, whom he had always valued highly, which must have stamped

him [[motifs/well|well]] in the esteem of every listener, had been followed by a little

[[concepts/history|history]] of his private life, which rendered him perfectly interesting

in the eyes of all the ladies. He had been engaged to Captain

Harville’s sister, and was now mourning her loss. They had been a year

or two waiting for fortune and promotion. Fortune came, his prize-money

as lieutenant being great; promotion, too, came at _last;_ but Fanny

Harville did not live to know it. She had died the preceding [[motifs/summer|summer]]

while he was at sea. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] believed it impossible for man

to be more attached to woman than poor Benwick had been to Fanny

Harville, or to be more deeply afflicted under the dreadful change. He

considered his disposition as of the sort which must suffer heavily,

uniting very strong feelings with quiet, serious, and retiring manners,

and a decided taste for reading, and sedentary pursuits. To finish the

interest of the story, the [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] between him and the Harvilles

seemed, if possible, augmented by the event which closed all their

views of alliance, and [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] was now living with them

entirely. Captain Harville had taken his present house for half a year;

his taste, and his health, and his fortune, all directing him to a

residence inexpensive, and by the sea; and the grandeur of the country,

and the retirement of Lyme in the [[motifs/winter|winter]], appeared exactly adapted to

[[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]]’s state of mind. The sympathy and good-will excited

towards [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] was very great.



“And yet,” said Anne to herself, as they now moved forward to meet the

party, “he has not, perhaps, a more sorrowing heart than I have. I

cannot believe his prospects so blighted for ever. He is younger than I

am; younger in feeling, if not in fact; younger as a man. He will rally

again, and be happy with another.”



They all met, and were introduced. Captain Harville was a tall, dark

man, with a sensible, benevolent countenance; a little lame; and from

strong features and want of health, looking much older than Captain

Wentworth. [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] looked, and was, the youngest of the three,

and, compared with either of them, a little man. He had a pleasing face

and a [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] air, just as he ought to have, and drew back from

conversation.



Captain Harville, though not equalling [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] in manners,

was a perfect gentleman, unaffected, warm, and obliging. Mrs Harville,

a degree less polished than her husband, seemed, however, to have the

same good feelings; and nothing could be more pleasant than their

[[motifs/desire|desire]] of considering the whole party as friends of their own, because

the friends of [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], or more kindly hospitable than their

entreaties for their all promising to dine with them. The dinner,

already ordered at the inn, was at last, though unwillingly, accepted

as a excuse; but they seemed almost hurt that [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] should

have brought any such party to Lyme, without considering it as a thing

of course that they should dine with them.



There was so much attachment to [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] in all this, and such

a bewitching charm in a degree of hospitality so uncommon, so unlike

the usual style of give-and-take invitations, and dinners of formality

and display, that Anne felt her spirits not likely to be benefited by

an increasing acquaintance among his brother-officers. “These would

have been all my friends,” was her thought; and she had to struggle

against a great tendency to lowness.



On quitting the Cobb, they all went in-doors with their new friends,

and found rooms so small as none but those who invite from the heart

could think capable of accommodating so many. Anne had a moment’s

astonishment on the subject herself; but it was soon lost in the

pleasanter feelings which sprang from the sight of all the ingenious

contrivances and nice arrangements of Captain Harville, to turn the

actual space to the best account, to supply the deficiencies of

lodging-house furniture, and defend the windows and doors against the

[[motifs/winter|winter]] storms to be expected. The varieties in the fitting-up of the

rooms, where the common necessaries provided by the owner, in the

Dove gli alberi della foresta e gli orti rigogliosamente cresciuti sono sparsi…

Dichiarare che molte generazioni devono essere passate da quando tutto ciò è iniziato…

La parziale erosione della scogliera ha preparato il terreno per tale stato di cose.

Un luogo in cui si presenta una scena così meravigliosa e incantevole…

Nessuna scena simile può eguagliare quelle leggendarie dell’Isola di Wight…

Questi luoghi meritano di essere visitati, e ancora una volta, per apprezzarne appieno il valore.

Lyme capì.



La compagnia di Uppercross che passa accanto al luogo ormai deserto…

Stanze dall’aspetto [[concepts/melancholy|melancolico]]; continuando a scendere, presto si trovarono.

Sulla riva del mare; e si sofferma lì, come tutti devono fare, ad ammirare…

Il primo ritorno al mare: chi mai avrebbe meritato di poterlo ammirare?

Proseguì verso il Cobb, che rappresentava lo stesso obiettivo per entrambi.

Il resoconto di [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]]: in una piccola casa, vicino alla base di una.

Sul vecchio molo, la cui data di costruzione è sconosciuta, si stabilirono i familiari Harville. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]]

Si recò da suo amico; gli altri continuarono per la loro strada, e lui invece…

Unisciti a loro sul Cobb.



Non erano affatto stanchi di meravigliarsi e ammirare… E nemmeno…

Sembra che Louisa avesse l'impressione che fossero passati molti mesi da quando si erano separati da [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]].

Quando lo videro avvicinarsi a loro, accompagnato da tre compagni, tutti in buona forma.

Conosciuti già, in base alla descrizione, come il Capitano e la Signora Harville… e un altro ancora.

[[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]], che stava soggiornando con loro.



[[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]] era stato, poco tempo fa, tenente di prima classe della nave Laconia.

E il resoconto che [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] aveva fatto di lui al suo ritorno.

Titolo:  
Dai tempi di Lyme… il suo caloroso elogio per lui come giovane eccezionale…

Un ufficiale che aveva sempre stimato molto… Il fatto che fosse coinvolto in questa situazione deve aver avuto un certo impatto…

Essendo molto apprezzato da tutti gli ascoltatori, fu seguito da un breve.

La [[concepts/history|storia]] della sua vita privata lo rendeva estremamente interessante.

Nel cuore di tutte le signore… Era fidanzato con il Capitano.

La sorella di Harville, che ora piangeva la sua perdita… Erano passati un anno.

“Uno o due in attesa di fortuna e promozione… La fortuna arrivò, e così anche il suo premio in denaro.”

Come tenente, ottenne grandi risultati; anche la promozione arrivò, alla fine… ma per Fanny fu diverso.

Harville non ebbe la possibilità di saperlo: era morta nell’[[motifs/summer|estate]] precedente.

Mentre si trovava in mare, [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] riteneva impossibile che un uomo.

Più attaccato a una donna di quanto povero Benwick lo fosse stato a Fanny

Harville… o meglio, colpito ancora più profondamente da quel terribile cambiamento. Lui.

Considerava la propria natura come di quel tipo che inevitabilmente soffre molto.

Unire sentimenti molto intensi a modi tranquilli, seri e riservati

E una marcata passione per la lettura, nonché per le attività sedentarie… Per concludere…

Per i motivi della storia, l’[[concepts/friendship|amicizia]] tra lui e la famiglia Harville è di grande importanza.

Sembrava che quell’evento, se possibile, potesse ancora rafforzare la situazione in cui si trovavano…

Punti di vista sull'alleanza, e ora [[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]] viveva con loro.

Del tutto. Il Capitano Harville aveva occupato la sua attuale >casa per mezzo anno;

“Il suo gusto, la sua salute e la sua fortuna lo guidano tutti verso…”

Residenza economica e situata vicino al mare… E la maestosità di questa regione…

E il ritiro di Lyme durante l’[[motifs/winter|inverno]] sembrava essere perfettamente adatto a.

Lo stato d’animo di [[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]]. La simpatia e la buona volontà che venivano manifestate.

Il suo affetto per [[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]] era davvero grande.



“Eppure…”, si disse Anne mentre avanzavano verso l’incontro.

“Partito… forse non c’è nessuno con un cuore più pieno di dolore del mio.”

Non riesco a credere che le sue prospettive siano destinate a rimanere distrutte per sempre… Lui è più giovane di me.

Più giovane nel sentire, se non nella realtà; più giovane come uomo… Si riprenderà.

Ancora una volta… e si sia felici con un altro.



Tutti si incontrarono e furono presentati. Il Capitano Harville era un uomo alto e di pelle scura…

Uomo dal volto sereno e benevolo; leggermente zoppo… e proveniente da…

Tratti forti ma mancanza di salute: sembra molto più vecchio del Capitano

Wentworth. [[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]] era il più giovane dei tre.

E, rispetto a entrambi, un uomo di statura bassa… Aveva un viso piacevole da vedere.

e con un’aria di [[concepts/melancholy|melancolia]], proprio come avrebbe dovuto essere, e si ritirò.

conversazione.



Il Capitano Harville, sebbene non eguagliasse il Capitano Wentworth per maniere.

Era un vero gentiluomo: naturale, cordiale e sempre disponibile ad aiutare gli altri. La signora Harville…

Un po’ meno raffinata del marito, sembrava tuttavia possedere…

Ancora le stesse belle sensazioni… E nulla potrebbe essere più piacevole di queste.

Il desiderio di considerare l’intera compagnia come amici propri, perché.

Gli amici di [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]], o più gentili e ospitalieri dei loro.

Inviti affinché tutti promettessero di cenare con loro. La cena…

Finalmente, sebbene con riluttanza, fu accettato.

Come scusa, ma sembravano quasi offesi dal fatto che [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] avesse detto così.

Hanno mai portato una simile compagnia a Lyme, senza considerarlo un fatto significativo?

Certo che dovrebbero pranzare con loro.



In tutto ciò c'era un legame così profondo con [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]], e tanto altro ancora.

Un incanto affascinante in un grado di ospitalità così raro, così diverso da tutto ciò che si vede solitamente…

Il solito stile di inviti basati su scambi reciproci e cene formali

E mostrava chiaramente che Anne riteneva che il suo umore non avrebbe certo migliorato…

“Un crescente rispetto da parte dei suoi colleghi ufficiali… Questi lo avrebbero…”

“Sono stati tutti i miei amici…”, pensò; e dovette lottare contro se stessa.

Nonostante una forte tendenza alla meschinità.



Entrando in casa con i loro nuovi amici

E trovarono stanze così piccole che solo coloro che invitano con il cuore potevano viverci.

“Potrebbe davvero ospitare così tante persone… Anne ci pensò per un momento.”

Sorpresa da parte della stessa interessata; ma presto svanì…

Piacevoli sensazioni nate alla vista di tutte quelle ingegnose soluzioni…

Titolo:  
Gli stratagemmi e le ingegnose soluzioni del Capitano Harville per…

Spazio reale sufficiente per colmare le lacune

Mobili per le locande e le case; difendere inoltre le finestre e le porte contro.

Si prevedono tempeste invernali. Le varietà utilizzate per i preparativi.

Stanze dove l’affittuatore fornisce i servizi essenziali



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11--part_03" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 11 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 11" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/faith,concept/hope,concept/nature,concept/resignation,concept/suffering,character/captain_benwick,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


common indifferent plight, were contrasted with some few articles of a

rare species of wood, excellently worked up, and with something curious

and valuable from all the distant countries Captain Harville had

visited, were more than amusing to Anne; connected as it all was with

his profession, the fruit of its labours, the effect of its influence

on his habits, the picture of repose and domestic happiness it

presented, made it to her a something more, or less, than

gratification.



Captain Harville was no reader; but he had contrived excellent

accommodations, and fashioned very pretty shelves, for a tolerable

collection of [[motifs/well|well]]-bound volumes, the property of [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]]. His

lameness prevented him from taking much exercise; but a mind of

usefulness and ingenuity seemed to furnish him with constant employment

within. He drew, he varnished, he carpentered, he glued; he made toys

for the children; he fashioned new netting-needles and pins with

improvements; and if everything else was done, sat down to his large

fishing-net at one corner of the room.



Anne thought she left great happiness behind her when they quitted the

house; and Louisa, by whom she found herself walking, burst forth into

raptures of admiration and delight on the character of the navy; their

friendliness, their brotherliness, their openness, their uprightness;

protesting that she was convinced of sailors having more worth and

warmth than any other set of men in England; that they only knew how to

live, and they only deserved to be respected and loved.



They went back to dress and dine; and so [[motifs/well|well]] had the scheme answered

already, that nothing was found amiss; though its being “so entirely

out of season,” and the “no thoroughfare of Lyme,” and the “no

expectation of company,” had brought many apologies from the heads of

the inn.



Anne found herself by this [[motifs/time|time]] growing so much more hardened to being

in [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s company than she had at first imagined could

ever be, that the sitting down to the same table with him now, and the

interchange of the common civilities attending on it (they never got

beyond), was become a mere nothing.



The nights were too dark for the ladies to meet again till the morrow,

but Captain Harville had promised them a visit in the evening; and he

came, bringing his friend also, which was more than had been expected,

it having been agreed that [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] had all the appearance of

being oppressed by the presence of so many strangers. He ventured among

them again, however, though his spirits certainly did not seem fit for

the mirth of the party in general.



While Captains Wentworth and Harville led the talk on one side of the

room, and by recurring to former days, supplied anecdotes in abundance

to occupy and entertain the others, it fell to Anne’s lot to be placed

rather apart with [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]]; and a very good impulse of her

[[concepts/nature|nature]] obliged her to begin an acquaintance with him. He was shy, and

disposed to abstraction; but the engaging mildness of her countenance,

and gentleness of her manners, soon had their effect; and Anne was [[motifs/well|well]]

repaid the first trouble of exertion. He was evidently a young man of

considerable taste in reading, though principally in poetry; and

besides the persuasion of having given him at least an evening’s

indulgence in the discussion of subjects, which his usual companions

had probably no concern in, she had the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of being of real use to

him in some suggestions as to the duty and benefit of struggling

against affliction, which had naturally grown out of their

conversation. For, though shy, he did not seem reserved; it had rather

the appearance of feelings glad to burst their usual restraints; and

having talked of poetry, the richness of the present age, and gone

through a brief comparison of opinion as to the first-rate poets,

trying to ascertain whether _Marmion_ or _The Lady of the Lake_ were to

be preferred, and how ranked the _Giaour_ and _The Bride of Abydos;_

and moreover, how the _Giaour_ was to be pronounced, he showed himself

so intimately acquainted with all the tenderest songs of the one poet,

and all the impassioned descriptions of hopeless agony of the other; he

repeated, with such tremulous feeling, the various lines which imaged a

broken heart, or a mind destroyed by wretchedness, and looked so

entirely as if he meant to be understood, that she ventured to [[concepts/hope|hope]] he

did not always read only poetry, and to say, that she thought it was

the misfortune of poetry to be seldom safely enjoyed by those who

enjoyed it completely; and that the strong feelings which alone could

estimate it truly were the very feelings which ought to taste it but

sparingly.



His looks shewing him not pained, but pleased with this allusion to his

situation, she was emboldened to go on; and feeling in herself the

right of seniority of mind, she ventured to recommend a larger

allowance of prose in his daily study; and on being requested to

particularize, mentioned such works of our best moralists, such

collections of the finest letters, such memoirs of characters of worth

and [[concepts/suffering|suffering]], as occurred to her at the moment as calculated to rouse

and fortify the mind by the highest precepts, and the strongest

examples of moral and religious endurances.



[[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]] listened attentively, and seemed grateful for the

interest implied; and though with a shake of the head, and sighs which

declared his little [[concepts/faith|faith]] in the efficacy of any books on grief like

his, noted down the names of those she recommended, and promised to

procure and read them.



When the evening was over, Anne could not but be amused at the idea of

her coming to Lyme to preach patience and [[concepts/resignation|resignation]] to a young man

whom she had never seen before; nor could she help fearing, on more

serious reflection, that, like many other great moralists and

preachers, she had been eloquent on a point in which her own conduct

would ill bear examination.
