CHAPTER XX.





Sir Walter, his two daughters, and Mrs Clay, were the earliest of all

their party at the rooms in the evening; and as Lady Dalrymple must be

waited for, they took their station by one of the fires in the Octagon

Room. But hardly were they so settled, when the door opened again, and

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] walked in alone. Anne was the nearest to him, and

making yet a little advance, she instantly spoke. He was preparing only

to bow and pass on, but her gentle “How do you do?” brought him out of

the straight line to stand near her, and make enquiries in return, in

spite of the formidable father and sister in the back ground. Their

being in the back ground was a support to Anne; she knew nothing of

their looks, and felt equal to everything which she believed right to

be done.



While they were speaking, a whispering between her father and Elizabeth

caught her ear. She could not distinguish, but she must guess the

subject; and on [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s making a distant bow, she

comprehended that her father had judged so [[motifs/well|well]] as to give him that

simple acknowledgement of acquaintance, and she was just in [[motifs/time|time]] by a

side glance to see a slight curtsey from Elizabeth herself. This,

though late, and reluctant, and ungracious, was yet better than

nothing, and her spirits improved.



After talking, however, of the weather, and Bath, and the concert,

their conversation began to [[motifs/flag|flag]], and so little was said at last, that

she was expecting him to go every moment, but he did not; he seemed in

no hurry to leave her; and presently with renewed spirit, with a little

smile, a little glow, he said—



“I have hardly seen you since our day at Lyme. I am afraid you must

have suffered from the shock, and the more from its not overpowering

you at the [[motifs/time|time]].”



She assured him that she had not.



“It was a frightful hour,” said he, “a frightful day!” and he passed

his hand across his eyes, as if the remembrance were still too painful,

but in a moment, half smiling again, added, “The day has produced some

effects however; has had some consequences which must be considered as

the very reverse of frightful. When you had the presence of mind to

suggest that Benwick would be the properest person to fetch a surgeon,

you could have little idea of his being eventually one of those most

concerned in her recovery.”



“Certainly I could have none. But it appears—I should [[concepts/hope|hope]] it would be

a very happy match. There are on both sides good principles and good

temper.”



“Yes,” said he, looking not exactly forward; “but there, I think, ends

the resemblance. With all my [[motifs/soul|soul]] I wish them happy, and rejoice over

every circumstance in favour of it. They have no difficulties to

contend with at [[motifs/home|home]], no opposition, no caprice, no delays. The

Musgroves are behaving like themselves, most honourably and kindly,

only anxious with true parental hearts to promote their daughter’s

comfort. All this is much, very much in favour of their happiness; more

than perhaps—”



He stopped. A sudden recollection seemed to occur, and to give him some

taste of that emotion which was reddening Anne’s cheeks and fixing her

eyes on the ground. After clearing his throat, however, he proceeded

thus—



“I confess that I do think there is a disparity, too great a disparity,

and in a point no less essential than mind. I regard Louisa Musgrove as

a very amiable, sweet-tempered girl, and not deficient in

understanding, but Benwick is something more. He is a clever man, a

reading man; and I confess, that I do consider his attaching himself to

her with some surprise. Had it been the effect of gratitude, had he

learnt to [[motifs/love|love]] her, because he believed her to be preferring him, it

would have been another thing. But I have no reason to suppose it so.

It seems, on the contrary, to have been a perfectly spontaneous,

untaught feeling on his side, and this surprises me. A man like him, in

his situation! with a heart pierced, wounded, almost broken! Fanny

Harville was a very superior creature, and his attachment to her was

indeed attachment. A man does not recover from such a devotion of the

heart to such a woman. He ought not; he does not.”



Either from the consciousness, however, that his friend had recovered,

or from other consciousness, he went no farther; and Anne who, in spite

of the agitated voice in which the latter part had been uttered, and in

spite of all the various noises of the room, the almost ceaseless slam

of the door, and ceaseless buzz of persons walking through, had

distinguished every word, was struck, gratified, confused, and

beginning to breathe very quick, and feel an hundred things in a

moment. It was impossible for her to enter on such a subject; and yet,

after a pause, feeling the necessity of speaking, and having not the

smallest wish for a total change, she only deviated so far as to say—



“You were a good while at Lyme, I think?”



“About a fortnight. I could not leave it till Louisa’s doing [[motifs/well|well]] was

quite ascertained. I had been too deeply concerned in the mischief to

be soon at peace. It had been my doing, solely mine. She would not have

been obstinate if I had not been weak. The country round Lyme is very

fine. I walked and rode a great deal; and the more I saw, the more I

found to admire.”



“I should very much like to see Lyme again,” said Anne.



“Indeed! I should not have supposed that you could have found anything

in Lyme to inspire such a feeling. The horror and distress you were

involved in, the stretch of mind, the wear of spirits! I should have

thought your last impressions of Lyme must have been strong disgust.”



“The last hours were certainly very painful,” replied Anne; “but when

[[motifs/pain|pain]] is over, the remembrance of it often becomes a pleasure. One does

not [[motifs/love|love]] a place the less for having suffered in it, unless it has been


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO XX.





Sir Walter, le sue due figlie e la signora Clay furono i primi tra tutti

La loro festa nelle stanze quella sera… e poiché Lady Dalrymple deve essere…

Aspettato il loro turno, presero posizione accanto a uno dei fuochi nell’Octagon.

Stanza… Ma appena si furono sistemati, la porta si aprì di nuovo.

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] entrò da solo. Anne era la più vicina a lui, e.

“Fatto un piccolo passo avanti, parlò immediatamente; lui, intanto, si stava solo preparando…”

“Per inchinarsi e andarsene… ma il suo gentile ‘Come sta?’ lo fece cambiare idea.”

La linea dritta per avvicinarsi a lei e porre delle domande a sua volta…

Nonostante la presenza minacciosa di un padre e di una sorella nel background…

Essere in secondo piano rappresentava un sostegno per Anne; lei non ne sapeva nulla.

I loro sguardi… e lei si sentì all’altezza di tutto ciò in cui credeva fosse giusto.

È fatta.



Mentre parlavano, si udì un sussurro tra suo padre ed Elizabeth.

Colpì il suo orecchio… Non riusciva a distinguere bene, ma doveva indovinare…

Soggetto. E mentre [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] faceva un inchino da lontano, lei.

Capì che suo padre aveva giudicato la situazione in modo così [[motifs/well|accurato]] da concedergli quella cosa.

Un semplice saluto di conoscenza, ed era proprio nel momento giusto.

“Un’occhiata di sguardo e vedo che Elizabeth stessa fa un leggero inchino… Questo…”

Anche se in ritardo, riluttante e scortese, era comunque meglio di…

Niente, e il suo umore migliorò.



Dopo aver parlato del tempo, di Bath e del concerto…

La loro conversazione iniziò a diventare noiosa; alla fine, si dissero così poco che.

Aspettava che se ne andasse da un momento all’altro, ma non lo fece; sembrava…

Non affrettarti ad andartene da lei… e presto, con nuovo spirito, un po’…

“Sorridi, una piccola luce…”, disse.



"Da quando siamo stati a Lyme, non ti ho quasi più visto… Temo che tu debba…"

Hanno sofferto per lo shock… e soprattutto perché non è stato troppo intenso.

Tu, in quel [[motifs/time|momento]].



Gli assicurò che non l'aveva fatto.



“Fu un’ora terribile… un giorno orribile!”, disse, e se ne andò.

La mano sulla fronte, come se quel ricordo fosse ancora troppo doloroso…

Ma dopo un momento, sorridendo di nuovo, aggiunse: “Questa giornata ha portato con sé alcune cose…”

Effetti comunque: ci sono state alcune conseguenze che devono essere prese in considerazione.

Il contrario di terribile… Quando si ha la presenza di spirito necessaria per…

Si suggerisce che Benwick sia la persona più adatta per andare a chiamare un chirurgo.

Mai avresti potuto immaginare che un giorno sarebbe diventato uno di quelli…

“Impegnata nella sua guarigione.”



“Certo, non ne avrei potuto avere alcuna. Ma sembra, dovrei [[concepts/hope|>sperare]] che possa essere, ”

Un matrimonio molto felice. Da entrambe le parti ci sono principi nobili e valori positivi…

“Temperamento”.



“Sì”, disse lui, senza sembrare particolarmente entusiasta; “ma credo che lì finisca tutto”.

Quella somiglianza. Con tutta la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]] desidero che siano felici e ne sono lieto.

Titolo:  
Tutte le circostanze sono a suo favore. Non hanno alcuna difficoltà…

Affrontare le cose in casa propria: nessuna opposizione, nessun capriccio, nessun ritardo.

I Musgrove si stanno comportando come al solito, con grande onore e gentilezza.

Solo genitori veramente premurosi desiderano promuovere il successo della propria figlia…

Comfort… Tutto ciò rappresenta un grande vantaggio per la loro felicità; molto di più ancora.

“Forse…”



Si fermò. Sembrava che gli fosse tornato in mente qualcosa all’improvviso, e questo gli aveva fornito qualche informazione importante.

Il sapore di quell’emozione che faceva arrossire le guance di Anne e la immobilizzava…

"Gli occhi fissi a terra... Dopo essersi schiarito la voce, però, proseguì."

Così…



“Confesso che ritengo effettivamente esista una disparità… una disparità troppo grande.”

E in un aspetto non meno essenziale della mente… Considero Louisa Musgrove come…

Una ragazza molto affabile e di buon carattere, e non mancava certo…

Un uomo intelligente… ma Benwick è qualcosa di più. È un uomo astuto, un…

Uomo di letture… e devo ammettere che trovo davvero interessante il fatto che si attacchi con tanta passione alle…

Con una certa sorpresa… Forse era un segno di gratitudine… O forse no?

Imparò ad [[motifs/love|amarla]], perché credeva che lei lo preferisse.

Sarebbe stato un altro discorso. Ma non ho alcun motivo per pensarlo.

Sembra, al contrario, che sia stato un gesto del tutto spontaneo.

Un sentimento spontaneo e inaspettato da parte sua… Questo mi sorprende. Un uomo come lui, davvero…

La sua situazione… con un cuore trafitto, ferito, quasi spezzato… Fanny

Harville era una creatura davvero superiore, e il suo attaccamento verso di lei…

Un attaccamento profondo… Un uomo non riesce mai a riprendersi da una tale devozione.

“Non dovrebbe… e in realtà non lo fa.”



O forse perché era consapevole che il suo amico si fosse ripreso…

O da un’altra coscienza… Non andò oltre; e Anne, nonostante…

Dalla voce agitata con cui era stata pronunciata l’ultima parte…

Nonostante tutti i vari rumori nella stanza, il continuo e incessante sbattere…

Il rumore continuo della porta che si apriva e chiudeva, unito al fruscio incessante delle persone che la attraversavano, creava un ambiente molto vivace…

Ogni parola era scelta con cura; suscitava emozioni diverse: ammirazione, soddisfazione… ma anche confusione.

Inizia a respirare molto velocemente e prova mille sensazioni diverse…

Momento… Era impossibile per lei affrontare un argomento del genere; eppure…

Dopo una pausa, sentendo la necessità di parlare… ma senza avere nulla da dire.

“Il desiderio più piccolo per un cambiamento totale… Lei si è allontanata dal suo obiettivo solo di poco, dicendo…”



“Sei stato via a Lyme per un bel po’, vero?”



“Circa quindici giorni. Non potevo andarmene finché Louisa non si fosse ripresa completamente.”

Del tutto certo… Ero troppo coinvolto in quella faccenda per poter dubitare.

“Riposerà presto in pace… Era stata tutta colpa mia, soltanto mia. Lei non avrebbe mai dovuto…”

Se non fossi stato debole, sarei stato ostinato… La zona intorno a Lyme è davvero…

Bene… Camminai e viaggiai molto; e più vedevo, più…

“Da ammirare senza dubbio.”



“Mi piacerebbe molto rivedere Lyme,” disse Anne.



"Certo! Non avrei mai pensato che fossi riuscito a trovarlo..."

In Lyme, per suscitare un tale sentimento… L’orrore e il dolore che avete provato…

“Immerso in quei pensieri, esausto nello spirito… Avrei dovuto…”

“Avrete sicuramente avuto un forte disgusto per le vostre ultime esperienze a Lyme…”



“Gli ultimi momenti sono stati sicuramente molto dolorosi“, rispose Anne; “ma quando…”

Il [[motifs/pain|dolore]] è passato; il ricordo di esso spesso diventa una fonte di piacere. Si fa.

Non si deve meno amare un luogo solo perché ci si è sofferti in esso, a meno che quel dolore non abbia avuto uno scopo positivo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_20--part_02" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 20 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 20" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/nature,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty,concept/friendship,concept/nature,concept/suffering,concept/vanity,concept/wonder,character/anne_elliot,character/captain_benwick,character/captain_wentworth,character/lady_russell"></span>


all [[concepts/suffering|suffering]], nothing but [[concepts/suffering|suffering]], which was by no means the case at

Lyme. We were only in anxiety and distress during the last two hours,

and previously there had been a great deal of enjoyment. So much

novelty and [[concepts/beauty|beauty]]! I have travelled so little, that every fresh place

would be interesting to me; but there is real [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] at Lyme; and in

short” (with a faint blush at some recollections), “altogether my

impressions of the place are very agreeable.”



As she ceased, the entrance door opened again, and the very party

appeared for whom they were waiting. “Lady Dalrymple, Lady Dalrymple,”

was the rejoicing sound; and with all the eagerness compatible with

anxious elegance, Sir Walter and his two ladies stepped forward to meet

her. Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret, escorted by Mr Elliot and

Colonel Wallis, who had happened to arrive nearly at the same instant,

advanced into the room. The others joined them, and it was a group in

which Anne found herself also necessarily included. She was divided

from [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]. Their interesting, almost too interesting

conversation must be broken up for a [[motifs/time|time]], but slight was the penance

compared with the happiness which brought it on! She had learnt, in the

last ten minutes, more of his feelings towards Louisa, more of all his

feelings than she dared to think of; and she gave herself up to the

demands of the party, to the needful civilities of the moment, with

exquisite, though agitated sensations. She was in good humour with all.

She had received ideas which disposed her to be courteous and kind to

all, and to pity every one, as being less happy than herself.



The delightful emotions were a little subdued, when on stepping back

from the group, to be joined again by [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], she saw that

he was gone. She was just in [[motifs/time|time]] to see him turn into the Concert

Room. He was gone; he had disappeared, she felt a moment’s regret. But

“they should meet again. He would look for her, he would find her out

before the evening were over, and at present, perhaps, it was as [[motifs/well|well]]

to be asunder. She was in need of a little interval for recollection.”



Upon [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]’s appearance soon afterwards, the whole party was

collected, and all that remained was to marshal themselves, and proceed

into the Concert Room; and be of all the consequence in their power,

draw as many eyes, excite as many whispers, and disturb as many people

as they could.



Very, very happy were both Elizabeth and [[characters/anne-elliot|Anne Elliot]] as they walked in.

Elizabeth arm in arm with Miss Carteret, and looking on the broad back

of the dowager Viscountess Dalrymple before her, had nothing to wish

for which did not seem within her reach; and Anne—but it would be an

insult to the [[concepts/nature|nature]] of Anne’s felicity, to draw any comparison between

it and her sister’s; the origin of one all selfish [[concepts/vanity|vanity]], of the other

all generous attachment.



Anne saw nothing, thought nothing of the brilliancy of the room. Her

happiness was from within. Her eyes were bright and her cheeks glowed;

but she knew nothing about it. She was thinking only of the last half

hour, and as they passed to their seats, her mind took a hasty range

over it. His choice of subjects, his expressions, and still more his

manner and look, had been such as she could see in only one light. His

opinion of Louisa Musgrove’s inferiority, an opinion which he had

seemed solicitous to give, his [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]], his feelings

as to a first, strong attachment; sentences begun which he could not

finish, his half averted eyes and more than half expressive glance,

all, all declared that he had a heart returning to her at least; that

anger, resentment, avoidance, were no more; and that they were

succeeded, not merely by [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] and regard, but by the tenderness

of the past. Yes, some share of the tenderness of the past. She could

not contemplate the change as implying less. He must [[motifs/love|love]] her.



These were thoughts, with their attendant visions, which occupied and

flurried her too much to leave her any power of observation; and she

passed along the room without having a glimpse of him, without even

trying to discern him. When their places were determined on, and they

were all properly arranged, she looked round to see if he should happen

to be in the same part of the room, but he was not; her eye could not

reach him; and the concert being just opening, she must consent for a

[[motifs/time|time]] to be happy in a humbler way.



The party was divided and disposed of on two contiguous benches: Anne

was among those on the foremost, and Mr Elliot had manœuvred so [[motifs/well|well]],

with the assistance of his friend Colonel Wallis, as to have a seat by

her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins, and the principal object

of Colonel Wallis’s gallantry, was quite contented.



Anne’s mind was in a most favourable state for the entertainment of the

evening; it was just occupation enough: she had feelings for the

tender, spirits for the gay, attention for the scientific, and patience

for the wearisome; and had never liked a concert better, at least

during the first act. Towards the close of it, in the interval

succeeding an Italian song, she explained the words of the song to Mr

Elliot. They had a concert bill between them.



“This,” said she, “is nearly the sense, or rather the meaning of the

words, for certainly the sense of an Italian [[motifs/love|love]]-song must not be

talked of, but it is as nearly the meaning as I can give; for I do not

pretend to understand the language. I am a very poor Italian scholar.”



“Yes, yes, I see you are. I see you know nothing of the matter. You

have only knowledge enough of the language to translate at sight these

inverted, transposed, curtailed Italian lines, into clear,


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

tutta [[concepts/suffering|sofferenza]], nient’altro che [[concepts/suffering|sofferenza]], il che non fu affatto il caso a

Lyme. Fummo in ansia e in angoscia soltanto nelle ultime due ore,

breve» (con un lieve rossore a qualche ricordo) «nel complesso le mie

Come ebbe finito, la porta d’ingresso si aprì di nuovo, e comparve proprio la comitiva

che aspettavano. «Lady Dalrymple, Lady Dalrymple!»

fu il suono festoso; e con tutta la premura compatibile con

un’ansiosa eleganza, Sir Walter e le sue due dame si fecero avanti per

conversazione doveva essere interrotta per un [[motifs/time|momento]], ma lieve era la penitenza

ultimi dieci minuti, più cose sui sentimenti di lui verso Louisa, più cose su tutti i suoi

sentimenti di quante osasse pensarne; e si abbandonò alle

esigenze della comitiva, alle cortesie necessarie del momento, con

sensazioni squisite, benché agitate. Era di buon umore con tutti.

Aveva ricevuto idee che la disponevano a essere cortese e gentile con

tutti, e a compatire ciascuno, come meno felice di lei.



Le deliziose emozioni si attenuarono un poco quando, ritraendosi

dal gruppo per essere di nuovo raggiunta dal [[characters/captain-wentworth|capitano Wentworth]], vide che

se n’era andato. Fece appena in [[motifs/time|tempo]] a vederlo svoltare nella sala

«si sarebbero incontrati di nuovo. L’avrebbe cercata, l’avrebbe trovata

prima che la serata finisse, e per ora, forse, era [[motifs/well|meglio]]

stare separati. Aveva bisogno di un piccolo intervallo per raccogliersi».



Con la comparsa di [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] poco dopo, tutta la compagnia fu

riunita, e non restava che disporsi in ordine e procedere

nella sala del concerto; e darsi tutta l’importanza in loro potere,

attirare quanti più sguardi, suscitare quanti più bisbigli e disturbare quante più persone

potessero.



Molto, molto felici erano entrambe, Elizabeth e [[characters/anne-elliot|Anne Elliot]], mentre entravano.

Elizabeth a braccetto con la signorina Carteret, e con davanti a sé l’ampia schiena

della viscontessa vedova Dalrymple, non aveva nulla da desiderare

essa e quella della sorella; l’origine dell’una tutta egoistica [[concepts/vanity|vanità]], quella dell’altra

tutto generoso attaccamento.



Anne non vide nulla, non pensò nulla dello splendore della sala. La sua

felicità veniva da dentro. Aveva gli occhi lucenti e le guance accese;

ma non ne sapeva nulla. Pensava soltanto all’ultima mezz’

ora, e mentre passavano ai loro posti, la sua mente ne fece un rapido

giro. La sua scelta degli argomenti, le sue espressioni, e ancor più i suoi

riguardo a un primo, forte attaccamento; frasi cominciate che non riusciva a

finire, gli occhi mezzo distolti e lo sguardo più che mezzo espressivo:

tutto, tutto dichiarava che egli aveva un cuore che almeno tornava a lei; che

la collera, il risentimento, l’evitarla, non c’erano più; e che erano stati

sostituiti non soltanto dall’[[concepts/friendship|amicizia]] e dalla stima, ma dalla tenerezza

del passato. Sì, una parte della tenerezza del passato. Non poteva

considerare quel mutamento come implicante meno di questo. Doveva [[motifs/love|amarla]].



Erano pensieri, con le visioni che li accompagnavano, che la occupavano e la

turbavano troppo per lasciarle alcuna facoltà di osservazione; ed ella

attraversò la sala senza scorgerlo un istante, senza nemmeno

cercare di distinguerlo. Quando i loro posti furono stabiliti, e furono

tutti convenientemente sistemati, si guardò intorno per vedere se per caso fosse

nella stessa parte della sala, ma non c’era; il suo occhio non riusciva a

raggiungerlo; e poiché il concerto stava appunto per cominciare, dovette acconsentire per il

[[motifs/time|momento]] a essere felice in modo più umile.



La comitiva fu divisa e sistemata su due panche contigue: Anne

era fra quelli della prima, e il signor Elliot aveva manovrato così [[motifs/well|bene]],

con l’aiuto del suo amico colonnello Wallis, da avere un posto accanto a

lei. La signorina Elliot, circondata dalle cugine, e principale oggetto

della galanteria del colonnello Wallis, era pienamente contenta.



L’animo di Anne era nella disposizione più favorevole per l’intrattenimento della

serata; era un’occupazione quanto bastava: aveva sentimento per le cose

tenere, brio per quelle allegre, attenzione per quelle dotte, e pazienza

per quelle noiose; e non le era mai piaciuto un concerto di più, almeno

durante il primo atto. Verso la fine di questo, nell’intervallo

che seguì una canzone italiana, spiegò le parole della canzone al signor

Elliot. Avevano fra loro un programma del concerto.



«Questo», disse, «è all’incirca il senso, o piuttosto il significato delle

parole, ché certo del senso di una canzone d’[[motifs/love|amore]] italiana non si deve

parlare, ma è quanto di più vicino al significato io possa dare; perché non

pretendo di capire la lingua. Sono una pessima conoscitrice dell’italiano».



«Sì, sì, vedo che lo siete. Vedo che non ne sapete nulla. Avete

conoscenza della lingua appena sufficiente a tradurre a prima vista questi

versi italiani invertiti, trasposti, mozzati, in un inglese chiaro,



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_20--part_03" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 20 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 20" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="topos/quest,motif/grave,motif/home,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/courage,concept/jealousy,concept/suffering,concept/truth,character/anne_elliot,character/captain_wentworth,character/lady_russell"></span>


comprehensible, elegant English. You need not say anything more of your

ignorance. Here is complete proof.”



“I will not oppose such kind politeness; but I should be sorry to be

examined by a real proficient.”



“I have not had the pleasure of visiting in Camden Place so long,”

replied he, “without knowing something of Miss [[characters/anne-elliot|Anne Elliot]]; and I do

regard her as one who is too modest for the world in general to be

aware of half her accomplishments, and too highly accomplished for

modesty to be natural in any other woman.”



“For shame! for shame! this is too much flattery. I forget what we are

to have next,” turning to the bill.



“Perhaps,” said Mr Elliot, speaking low, “I have had a longer

acquaintance with your character than you are aware of.”



“Indeed! How so? You can have been acquainted with it only since I came

to Bath, excepting as you might hear me previously spoken of in my own

family.”



“I knew you by report long before you came to Bath. I had heard you

described by those who knew you intimately. I have been acquainted with

you by character many years. Your person, your disposition,

accomplishments, manner; they were all present to me.”



Mr Elliot was not disappointed in the interest he hoped to raise. No

one can withstand the charm of such a mystery. To have been described

long ago to a recent acquaintance, by nameless people, is irresistible;

and Anne was all curiosity. She wondered, and questioned him eagerly;

but in vain. He delighted in being asked, but he would not tell.



“No, no, some [[motifs/time|time]] or other, perhaps, but not now. He would mention no

names now; but such, he could assure her, had been the fact. He had

many years ago received such a description of Miss [[characters/anne-elliot|Anne Elliot]] as had

inspired him with the highest idea of her merit, and excited the

warmest curiosity to know her.”



Anne could think of no one so likely to have spoken with partiality of

her many years ago as the Mr Wentworth of Monkford, [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s

brother. He might have been in Mr Elliot’s company, but she had not

[[concepts/courage|courage]] to ask the question.



“The name of [[characters/anne-elliot|Anne Elliot]],” said he, “has long had an interesting sound

to me. Very long has it possessed a charm over my fancy; and, if I

dared, I would breathe my wishes that the name might never change.”



Such, she believed, were his words; but scarcely had she received their

sound, than her attention was caught by other sounds immediately behind

her, which rendered every thing else trivial. Her father and Lady

Dalrymple were speaking.



“A [[motifs/well|well]]-looking man,” said Sir Walter, “a very [[motifs/well|well]]-looking man.”



“A very fine young man indeed!” said Lady Dalrymple. “More air than one

often sees in Bath. Irish, I dare say.”



“No, I just know his name. A bowing acquaintance. Wentworth; Captain

Wentworth of the navy. His sister married my tenant in Somersetshire,

the Croft, who rents Kellynch.”



Before Sir Walter had reached this point, Anne’s eyes had caught the

right direction, and distinguished [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] standing among a

cluster of men at a little distance. As her eyes fell on him, his

seemed to be withdrawn from her. It had that appearance. It seemed as

if she had been one moment too late; and as long as she dared observe,

he did not look again: but the performance was recommencing, and she

was forced to seem to restore her attention to the orchestra and look

straight forward.



When she could give another glance, he had moved away. He could not

have come nearer to her if he would; she was so surrounded and shut in:

but she would rather have caught his eye.



Mr Elliot’s speech, too, distressed her. She had no longer any

inclination to talk to him. She wished him not so near her.



The first act was over. Now she hoped for some beneficial change; and,

after a period of nothing-saying amongst the party, some of them did

decide on going in [[topoi/quest|quest]] of tea. Anne was one of the few who did not

choose to move. She remained in her seat, and so did [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]; but

she had the pleasure of getting rid of Mr Elliot; and she did not mean,

whatever she might feel on [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]’s account, to shrink from

conversation with [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], if he gave her the opportunity.

She was persuaded by [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]’s countenance that she had seen him.



He did not come however. Anne sometimes fancied she discerned him at a

distance, but he never came. The anxious interval wore away

unproductively. The others returned, the room filled again, benches

were reclaimed and repossessed, and another hour of pleasure or of

penance was to be sat out, another hour of music was to give delight or

the gapes, as real or affected taste for it prevailed. To Anne, it

chiefly wore the prospect of an hour of agitation. She could not quit

that room in peace without seeing [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] once more, without

the interchange of one friendly look.



In re-settling themselves there were now many changes, the result of

which was favourable for her. Colonel Wallis declined sitting down

again, and Mr Elliot was invited by Elizabeth and Miss Carteret, in a

manner not to be refused, to sit between them; and by some other

removals, and a little scheming of her own, Anne was enabled to place

herself much nearer the end of the bench than she had been before, much

more within reach of a passer-by. She could not do so, without

comparing herself with Miss Larolles, the inimitable Miss Larolles; but

still she did it, and not with much happier effect; though by what

seemed prosperity in the shape of an early abdication in her next

neighbours, she found herself at the very end of the bench before the

concert closed.



Such was her situation, with a vacant space at hand, when Captain

Wentworth was again in sight. She saw him not far off. He saw her too;

yet he looked [[motifs/grave|grave]], and seemed irresolute, and only by very slow

degrees came at last near enough to speak to her. She felt that

something must be the matter. The change was indubitable. The

difference between his present air and what it had been in the Octagon

Room was strikingly great. Why was it? She thought of her father, of

[[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]. Could there have been any unpleasant glances? He began by

speaking of the concert gravely, more like the [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] of

Uppercross; owned himself disappointed, had expected singing; and in

short, must confess that he should not be sorry when it was over. Anne

replied, and spoke in defence of the performance so [[motifs/well|well]], and yet in

allowance for his feelings so pleasantly, that his countenance

improved, and he replied again with almost a smile. They talked for a

few minutes more; the improvement held; he even looked down towards the

bench, as if he saw a place on it [[motifs/well|well]] worth occupying; when at that

moment a touch on her shoulder obliged Anne to turn round. It came from

Mr Elliot. He begged her pardon, but she must be applied to, to explain

Italian again. Miss Carteret was very anxious to have a general idea of

what was next to be sung. Anne could not refuse; but never had she

sacrificed to politeness with a more [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] spirit.



A few minutes, though as few as possible, were inevitably consumed; and

when her own mistress again, when able to turn and look as she had done

before, she found herself accosted by [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]], in a reserved

yet hurried sort of farewell. “He must wish her good [[motifs/night|night]]; he was

going; he should get [[motifs/home|home]] as fast as he could.”



“Is not this song worth staying for?” said Anne, suddenly struck by an

idea which made her yet more anxious to be encouraging.



“No!” he replied impressively, “there is nothing worth my staying for;”

and he was gone directly.



[[concepts/jealousy|Jealousy]] of Mr Elliot! It was the only intelligible motive. Captain

Wentworth jealous of her affection! Could she have believed it a week

ago; three hours ago! For a moment the gratification was exquisite.

But, alas! there were very different thoughts to succeed. How was such

[[concepts/jealousy|jealousy]] to be quieted? How was the [[concepts/truth|truth]] to reach him? How, in all the

peculiar disadvantages of their respective situations, would he ever

learn of her real sentiments? It was misery to think of Mr Elliot’s

attentions. Their evil was incalculable.
