E dopo aver fatto del suo meglio, attende l’evento con la massima calma possibile.

Possibile… E dopotutto, il momento in cui avrebbe più bisogno di mantenere la calma sarebbe proprio in quel momento.

Quella parte della mente che non poteva essere aperta a [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]]; in.

Quel flusso di ansie e paure che doveva appartenerle esclusivamente a lei.



Arrivata a [[motifs/home|>casa]], scoprì di essere riuscita, come aveva intenzionato, a fuggire.

Incontrare il signor Elliot: aveva telefonato e trascorso un lungo pomeriggio da loro.

Visita… Ma appena si fu congratulata con se stessa e si sentì al sicuro, ecco che…

Sentì dire che sarebbe tornato quella sera stessa.



“Non avevo affatto l’intenzione di chiederglielo”, disse Elizabeth.

Cura apparentemente negligente, “ma ha dato così tanti indizi; dice la signora Clay…”

“Il minimo indispensabile.”



“Certo, lo dico davvero: nella mia vita non ho mai visto nessuno sforzarsi così tanto per scrivere…”

Un invito. Povero uomo! Mi dispiaceva davvero per lui. Per te, intendo.

“La spietata sorella maggiore, la signorina Anne, sembra decisa ad essere crudele.”



“Oh!”, esclamò Elizabeth, “Sono ormai troppo abituata a questo gioco…”

Viene presto sopraffatto dalle allusioni di un gentiluomo… Tuttavia, quando capii come…

Si pentiva troppo di dover perdere mio padre in quel momento

La mattina seguente, cedetti immediatamente, perché in realtà non avrei mai potuto omettere nulla…

L’opportunità di far incontrare lui e Sir Walter… Sembra proprio che sia il caso.

Molto vantaggioso stare insieme gli uni agli altri; ognuno si comporta in modo così piacevole.

“Il signor Elliot alza lo sguardo con grande rispetto.”



“Davvero delizioso!” esclamò la signora Clay, senza però osare girarsi.

“Gli occhi di lui assomigliano molto a quelli di suo padre… Carissima signorina Elliot, possa…”

“Non dici mai ‘padre e figlio’?”



“Oh! Non impongo alcun divieto sulle parole di nessun [[concepts/body|corpo]]. Se volete avere simili idee,!”

Ma, per la mia parola, a malapena mi rendo conto che lui mi stia prestando attenzione…

“Al di là di ciò che gli altri uomini hanno”.



“Mia cara signorina Elliot!”, esclamò la signora Clay, alzando le mani e gli occhi.

e nascondendo tutto il resto della sua meraviglia in un comodo [[motifs/silence|silenzio]].



“Beh, mia cara Penelope, non c’è bisogno che tu ti preoccupi così tanto per lui. Io ho, ”

Invitalo, sai… L’ho congedato sorridendo. Quando ho scoperto che era…

Andrà davvero dai suoi amici a Thornberry Park per tutta la giornata

“Domani… provai compassione per lui.”



Anne ammirava la notevole capacità dell’amica di recitare così bene

Piacere come faceva lei, nell’attesa e nel momento stesso dell’arrivo…

La persona stessa la cui presenza sta sicuramente interferendo con lei

Obiettivo principale… Era impossibile, ma la signora Clay doveva odiare quella vista.

Il signor Elliot… eppure riusciva ad assumere un’espressione estremamente gentile e tranquilla.

E sembrano piuttosto soddisfatti della licenza ridotta concessa per dedicarsi…

Solo la metà di ciò che avrebbe voluto dare a Sir Walter…

In caso contrario.



Per Anne stessa fu estremamente doloroso vedere entrare il signor Elliot.

“La stanza… E era davvero doloroso vederlo avvicinarsi e parlarle.” Lei aveva…

Non è mai stato possibile dubitare della sua sincerità…

Ora vedeva insincerità in tutto… La sua attenta deferenza verso di lei…

“Padre… il suo modo di parlare, diverso da prima, risultava odioso; e quando lei…”

Pensando al suo comportamento crudele verso la signora Smith, lei faticava a sopportarlo.

La vista dei suoi sorrisi attuali e della sua dolcezza, o il suono delle sue parole…

Sentimenti artificialmente generati.



Un cambiamento di comportamento che potrebbe provocare…

Remprover da parte sua… Per lei era un’ottima opportunità per scappare da tutto.

Indagine o clamore… Ma la sua intenzione era quella di rimanere decisamente calma.

Un titolo che rifletta il modo in cui le loro azioni dovrebbero essere in armonia con la loro relazione… e per tornare indietro, come se fosse necessario farlo.

Con la massima discrezione possibile, quelle poche azioni di intimità non necessarie che aveva compiuto…

Guidata gradualmente in quella direzione… Fu quindi più cauta, e molto di più.

Fantastico, allora quella notte precedente era stata davvero speciale per lei.



Voleva risvegliare di nuovo la sua curiosità riguardo al modo e al luogo in cui avrebbe potuto farlo.

Ho sentito parlare bene di lei in passato; desideravo molto poter essere soddisfatto da ciò che avrei visto o ascoltato riguardo a lei.

Ancora tentazioni… ma il fascino era svanito: si rese conto che quel calore e…

L'animazione di una sala pubblica risultò necessaria per stimolare il carattere riservato di suo cugino…

La [[concepts/vanity|vanità]]; almeno scoprì che in quel momento non era il caso di agire in quel modo, da parte di nessuno.

Titolo:  
Quei tentativi che poté intraprendere nonostante le pretese troppo pressanti…

Gli altri… Lui non si rese nemmeno conto che in quel momento quel soggetto stesse agendo esattamente così.

Contrariamente ai suoi interessi, questo fatto le fece subito venire in mente tutte quelle cose…

Le parti del suo comportamento che erano le meno giustificabili.



Un certo soddisfazione provò nel constatare che lui stava davvero per andarsene

La mattina seguente, si alzò presto per fare il bagno e poi se ne andò…

La maggior parte di due giorni… Fu nuovamente invitato a Camden Place…

La sera del suo ritorno; ma dal Giovedì alla sera di sabato.

L’assenza era certa. Era già abbastanza grave che una signora Clay dovesse sempre…

Prima di lei… ma che nel loro gruppo dovesse aggiungersi anche un ipocrita ancora più profondo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_22--part_02" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 22 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 22" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/deception,concept/history,form/history,character/captain_benwick,character/lady_russell"></span>


seemed the destruction of everything like peace and comfort. It was so

humiliating to reflect on the constant [[concepts/deception|deception]] practised on her

father and Elizabeth; to consider the various sources of mortification

preparing for them! Mrs Clay’s selfishness was not so complicate nor so

revolting as his; and Anne would have compounded for the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] at

once, with all its evils, to be clear of Mr Elliot’s subtleties in

endeavouring to prevent it.



On Friday morning she meant to go very early to [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]], and

accomplish the necessary communication; and she would have gone

directly after breakfast, but that Mrs Clay was also going out on some

obliging purpose of saving her sister trouble, which determined her to

wait till she might be safe from such a companion. She saw Mrs Clay

fairly off, therefore, before she began to talk of spending the morning

in Rivers Street.



“Very [[motifs/well|well]],” said Elizabeth, “I have nothing to send but my [[motifs/love|love]]. Oh!

you may as [[motifs/well|well]] take back that tiresome book she would lend me, and

pretend I have read it through. I really cannot be plaguing myself for

ever with all the new poems and states of the nation that come out.

[[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] quite bores one with her new publications. You need not

tell her so, but I thought her dress hideous the other [[motifs/night|night]]. I used to

think she had some taste in dress, but I was ashamed of her at the

concert. Something so formal and _arrangé_ in her air! and she sits so

upright! My best [[motifs/love|love]], of course.”



“And mine,” added Sir Walter. “Kindest regards. And you may say, that I

mean to call upon her soon. Make a civil message; but I shall only

leave my card. Morning visits are never fair by women at her [[motifs/time|time]] of

life, who make themselves up so little. If she would only wear rouge

she would not be afraid of being seen; but last [[motifs/time|time]] I called, I

observed the blinds were let down immediately.”



While her father spoke, there was a knock at the door. Who could it be?

Anne, remembering the preconcerted visits, at all hours, of Mr Elliot,

would have expected him, but for his known engagement seven miles off.

After the usual period of suspense, the usual sounds of approach were

heard, and “Mr and Mrs Charles Musgrove” were ushered into the room.



Surprise was the strongest emotion raised by their appearance; but Anne

was really glad to see them; and the others were not so sorry but that

they could put on a decent air of welcome; and as soon as it became

clear that these, their nearest relations, were not arrived with any

views of accommodation in that house, Sir Walter and Elizabeth were

able to rise in cordiality, and do the honours of it very [[motifs/well|well]]. They

were come to Bath for a few days with Mrs Musgrove, and were at the

White Hart. So much was pretty soon understood; but till Sir Walter and

Elizabeth were walking Mary into the other drawing-room, and regaling

themselves with her admiration, Anne could not draw upon Charles’s

brain for a regular [[concepts/history|history]] of their coming, or an explanation of some

smiling hints of particular business, which had been ostentatiously

dropped by Mary, as [[motifs/well|well]] as of some apparent confusion as to whom their

party consisted of.



She then found that it consisted of Mrs Musgrove, Henrietta, and

Captain Harville, beside their two selves. He gave her a very plain,

intelligible account of the whole; a narration in which she saw a great

deal of most characteristic proceeding. The scheme had received its

first impulse by Captain Harville’s wanting to come to Bath on

business. He had begun to talk of it a week ago; and by way of doing

something, as shooting was over, Charles had proposed coming with him,

and Mrs Harville had seemed to like the idea of it very much, as an

advantage to her husband; but Mary could not bear to be left, and had

made herself so unhappy about it, that for a day or two everything

seemed to be in suspense, or at an end. But then, it had been taken up

by his father and mother. His mother had some old friends in Bath whom

she wanted to see; it was thought a good opportunity for Henrietta to

come and buy wedding-clothes for herself and her sister; and, in short,

it ended in being his mother’s party, that everything might be

comfortable and easy to Captain Harville; and he and Mary were included

in it by way of general convenience. They had arrived late the [[motifs/night|night]]

before. Mrs Harville, her children, and [[characters/captain-benwick|Captain Benwick]], remained with

Mr Musgrove and Louisa at Uppercross.



Anne’s only surprise was, that affairs should be in forwardness enough

for Henrietta’s wedding-clothes to be talked of. She had imagined such

difficulties of fortune to exist there as must prevent the [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]

from being near at hand; but she learned from Charles that, very

recently, (since Mary’s last letter to herself), Charles Hayter had

been applied to by a friend to hold a living for a youth who could not

possibly claim it under many years; and that on the strength of his

present income, with almost a certainty of something more permanent

long before the term in question, the two families had consented to the

young people’s wishes, and that their [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] was likely to take place

in a few months, quite as soon as Louisa’s. “And a very good living it

was,” Charles added: “only five-and-twenty miles from Uppercross, and

in a very fine country: fine part of Dorsetshire. In the centre of some

of the best preserves in the kingdom, surrounded by three great

proprietors, each more careful and jealous than the other; and to two

of the three at least, Charles Hayter might get a special

recommendation. Not that he will value it as he ought,” he observed,

“Charles is too cool about sporting. That’s the worst of him.”



“I am extremely glad, indeed,” cried Anne, “particularly glad that this

should happen; and that of two sisters, who both deserve equally [[motifs/well|well]],


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Sembrava la distruzione di tutto ciò che rappresentava pace e conforto… Era davvero così.

È umiliante riflettere sulla costante [[concepts/deception|inganno]] che le viene inflitto.

Padre ed Elisabetta: considerare le varie fonti di umiliazione

“Preparandosi per loro… L’egoismo di Mrs Clay non era così complicato, né così…”

Rivoluzionario com'era lui. E Anne avrebbe voluto sistemare le cose per il [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]].

Una volta, nonostante tutti i suoi mali… per liberarsi dalle sottigliezze di Mr. Elliot.

Cercando di impedirlo.



Venerdì mattina aveva intenzione di andare molto presto da [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]], e.

Riuscire a stabilire la comunicazione necessaria… e poi sarebbe partita.

Subito dopo colazione, ma anche la signora Clay aveva intenzione di uscire…

Il nobile scopo di evitare problemi a sua sorella… che la spinse a…

Aspetta che possa essere al sicuro da un compagno del genere… Vide la signora Clay.

Quindi, prima ancora che iniziasse a parlare di trascorrere la mattina insieme…

in Rivers Street.



“Molto bene,” disse Elizabeth, “non ho nulla da inviare se non il mio [[motifs/love|amore]]. Oh!”

Puoi benissimo riprenderti quel noioso libro che mi aveva prestato.

Fingo di averlo letto tutto… Non posso davvero tormentarmi così.

Ogni volta, con tutti i nuovi poemi e le notizie sullo stato della nazione che vengono pubblicati.

[[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] con le sue nuove pubblicazioni finisce per noiare davvero chi la ascolta. Non c’è bisogno di.

Dille così, ma quella [[motifs/night|notte]] ho pensato che il suo vestito fosse orribile. Io di solito.

Pensavo che avesse un certo gusto in fatto di abbigliamento, ma mi vergognavo di lei in quel momento…

Concerto… Qualcosa di così formale e ben organizzato nel suo modo di comportarsi… E lei se ne siede lì, con quell’aria…

Dritto in piedi! La mia migliore [[motifs/love|amata]], naturalmente.”



“E anche il mio,” aggiunse Sir Walter. “I miei più cordiali saluti. E potete dire che io…”

Intenderò contattarla presto. Invierò un messaggio cortese, ma…

Lasciami il tuo numero di telefono. Le visite mattutine, da parte delle donne, a quell’ora della giornata, non sono mai appropriate.

“La vita… coloro che si danno così poco valore. Se solo indossasse del rossetto…”

Non avrebbe avuto paura di essere vista; ma l’ultima [[motifs/time|volta]] che ho chiamato.

“Si notò che le tende venivano immediatamente abbassate.”



Mentre suo padre parlava, si sentì bussare alla porta. Chi poteva essere?

Anne: i continui e premeditati visite del signor Elliot, in qualsiasi ora del giorno…

Avrei potuto aspettarmelo, se non fosse stato per il suo conosciuto impegno a sette miglia di distanza.

Dopo il solito periodo di attesa, si udirono i soliti rumori che annunciavano l’arrivo…

Sentirono bussare, e “il signor e la signora Charles Musgrove” furono fatti entrare nella stanza.



La sorpresa fu l’emozione più forte che suscitò la loro apparizione; ma Anne…

Ero davvero felice di vederli; gli altri, invece, non erano così dispiaciuti…

Potrebbero mostrare un minimo di accoglienza cordiale… e non appena ciò avvenisse…

“Si chiarisce che questi, i loro parenti più stretti, non erano arrivati insieme ad altri…”

Le opinioni riguardo alle sistemazioni abitative in quella >casa, Sir Walter ed Elizabeth erano.

In grado di comportarsi con cordialità e di svolgere tali onori in modo molto [[motifs/well|buono]]. Loro.

Erano venuti a Bath per qualche giorno con la signora Musgrove e si trovavano…

White Hart. Molto presto si capì tutto; ma fino a quando Sir Walter e…

Elizabeth accompagnava Mary nell’altra sala da pranzo, intrattendendola con storie interessanti…

Con l’ammirazione che provava per lui, Anne non riusciva a contare sull’appoggio di Charles…

Un cervello capace di fornire una[[concepts/history|storia]] completa del loro arrivo, o una spiegazione per alcuni aspetti.

Titolo:  
Suggerimenti sorridenti riguardo a affari particolari, che erano stati ostentatamente…

Passò a trovarli Mary; sembrava esserci un po' di confusione su chi fosse il loro.

La festa era composta da.



Lei scoprì che erano comprese la signora Musgrove, Henrietta e…

Capitano Harville… solo loro due. Le rivolse uno sguardo molto semplice, diretto.

Una spiegazione chiara e completa di tutto; un resoconto nel quale lei vide qualcosa di grandioso

Titolo:  
Il procedimento più caratteristico… Il piano aveva ricevuto il suo…

Il primo impulso del Capitano Harville fu quello di recarsi a Bath…

Affari… Ne aveva iniziato a parlare una settimana fa; e, per così dire,…

Dopo che la sparatoria era finita, Charles gli aveva proposto di andare con lui.

E sembrava che anche la signora Harville apprezzasse molto l’idea.

Un vantaggio per suo marito… ma Mary non riusciva a sopportare l’idea di essere lasciata sola, e così…

Si rese così infelice a causa di questo, che per un giorno o due tutto…

Sembrava essere sospeso… o forse al termine. Ma poi, la storia è ripresa.

Cresciuto da suo padre e sua madre… Sua madre aveva alcune vecchie amiche a Bath…

Voleva vederlo; si riteneva che fosse un’ottima opportunità per Henrietta…

Vieni a comprare abiti da sposa per sé e sua sorella; insomma…

Finì per diventare la festa di sua madre… affinché tutto potesse andare come previsto.

“Comodo e facile da usare per il Capitano Harville… Lui e Mary ne furono entrambi benefici.”

Per comodità generale, vi erano entrati. Erano arrivati tardi, quella [[motifs/night|notte]].

Prima di allora, la signora Harville, i suoi figli e il [[characters/captain-benwick|Capitano Benwick]] rimasero insieme.

Il signor Musgrove e Louisa a Uppercross.



L’unica sorpresa di Anne fu che le cose fossero già così avvanzate.

Per le vesti da sposa di Henrietta… ne parlavano tutti. Lei se l’era immaginata proprio così.

Le difficoltà della vita dovrebbero impedire che quel [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] avvenga.

Da essere sempre a portata di mano… ma imparò da Charles che, in realtà, non è così semplice.

Di recente, da quando Mary gli aveva scritto l’ultima lettera, Charles Hayter…

Un amico me ne ha parlato per aiutare un giovane che non riusciva a…

Titolo:  
È possibile rivendicarlo dopo molti anni… e questo grazie alle sue ragioni.

Entrate attuali, con la quasi certezza di ottenere qualcosa di più duraturo

Molto prima che venisse coniato quel termine, le due famiglie avevano già acconsentito…

I desideri dei giovani, e il fatto che il loro [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]] fosse molto probabile che avvenisse.

“In pochi mesi, esattamente come per Louisa… E una vita davvero molto agiata.”

“Era situata”, aggiunse Charles, “solo a venticinque miglia da Uppercross…”

In una regione davvero incantevole: la bellissima parte del Dorsetshire, nel cuore di un luogo meraviglioso…

Dei migliori prodotti conservati del regno, circondati da tre grandi…

Proprietari, ognuno più attento e geloso dell’altro… e due di loro in particolare.

Almeno di questi tre, Charles Hayter potrebbe ricevere un trattamento speciale.

“Una raccomandazione… Ma non è certo che la prenderà in considerazione come dovrebbe”, osservò.

“Charles è troppo disinteressato allo sport… Questo è il suo peggior lato.”



“Sono davvero estremamente felice”, esclamò Anne, “soprattutto felice che questo…”

Dovrebbe accadere. E lo stesso vale per due sorelle che entrambe meritano allo stesso modo di essere trattate bene.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_22--part_03" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 22 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 22" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/autumn,motif/journey,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/suffering,concept/vanity,character/lady_russell"></span>


and who have always been such good friends, the pleasant prospect of

one should not be dimming those of the other—that they should be so

equal in their prosperity and comfort. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] your father and mother

are quite happy with regard to both.”



“Oh! yes. My father would be [[motifs/well|well]] pleased if the gentlemen were richer,

but he has no other fault to find. Money, you know, coming down with

money—two daughters at once—it cannot be a very agreeable operation,

and it streightens him as to many things. However, I do not mean to say

they have not a right to it. It is very fit they should have daughters’

shares; and I am sure he has always been a very kind, liberal father to

me. Mary does not above half like Henrietta’s match. She never did, you

know. But she does not do him justice, nor think enough about Winthrop.

I cannot make her attend to the value of the property. It is a very

fair match, as times go; and I have liked Charles Hayter all my life,

and I shall not leave off now.”



“Such excellent parents as Mr and Mrs Musgrove,” exclaimed Anne,

“should be happy in their children’s marriages. They do everything to

confer happiness, I am sure. What a blessing to young people to be in

such hands! Your father and mother seem so totally free from all those

ambitious feelings which have led to so much misconduct and misery,

both in young and old. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you think Louisa perfectly recovered

now?”



He answered rather hesitatingly, “Yes, I believe I do; very much

recovered; but she is altered; there is no running or jumping about, no

laughing or dancing; it is quite different. If one happens only to shut

the door a little hard, she starts and wriggles like a young dab-chick

in the [[motifs/water|water]]; and Benwick sits at her elbow, reading verses, or

whispering to her, all day long.”



Anne could not help laughing. “That cannot be much to your taste, I

know,” said she; “but I do believe him to be an excellent young man.”



“To be sure he is. Nobody doubts it; and I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you do not think I am

so illiberal as to want every man to have the same objects and

pleasures as myself. I have a great value for Benwick; and when one can

but get him to talk, he has plenty to say. His reading has done him no

harm, for he has fought as [[motifs/well|well]] as read. He is a brave fellow. I got

more acquainted with him last Monday than ever I did before. We had a

famous set-to at rat-hunting all the morning in my father’s great

barns; and he played his part so [[motifs/well|well]] that I have liked him the better

ever since.”



Here they were interrupted by the absolute necessity of Charles’s

following the others to admire mirrors and china; but Anne had heard

enough to understand the present state of Uppercross, and rejoice in

its happiness; and though she sighed as she rejoiced, her sigh had none

of the ill-will of envy in it. She would certainly have risen to their

blessings if she could, but she did not want to lessen theirs.



The visit passed off altogether in high good humour. Mary was in

excellent spirits, enjoying the gaiety and the change, and so [[motifs/well|well]]

satisfied with the [[motifs/journey|journey]] in her mother-in-law’s carriage with four

horses, and with her own complete independence of Camden Place, that

she was exactly in a temper to admire everything as she ought, and

enter most readily into all the superiorities of the house, as they

were detailed to her. She had no demands on her father or sister, and

her consequence was just enough increased by their handsome

drawing-rooms.



Elizabeth was, for a short [[motifs/time|time]], [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] a good deal. She felt that

Mrs Musgrove and all her party ought to be asked to dine with them; but

she could not bear to have the difference of style, the reduction of

servants, which a dinner must betray, witnessed by those who had been

always so inferior to the Elliots of Kellynch. It was a struggle

between propriety and [[concepts/vanity|vanity]]; but [[concepts/vanity|vanity]] got the better, and then

Elizabeth was happy again. These were her internal persuasions: “Old

fashioned notions; country hospitality; we do not profess to give

dinners; few people in Bath do; Lady Alicia never does; did not even

ask her own sister’s family, though they were here a month: and I dare

say it would be very inconvenient to Mrs Musgrove; put her quite out of

her way. I am sure she would rather not come; she cannot feel easy with

us. I will ask them all for an evening; that will be much better; that

will be a novelty and a treat. They have not seen two such drawing

rooms before. They will be delighted to come to-morrow evening. It

shall be a regular party, small, but most elegant.” And this satisfied

Elizabeth: and when the invitation was given to the two present, and

promised for the absent, Mary was as completely satisfied. She was

particularly asked to meet Mr Elliot, and be introduced to Lady

Dalrymple and Miss Carteret, who were fortunately already engaged to

come; and she could not have received a more gratifying attention. Miss

Elliot was to have the [[concepts/honour|honour]] of calling on Mrs Musgrove in the course

of the morning; and Anne walked off with Charles and Mary, to go and

see her and Henrietta directly.



Her plan of sitting with [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] must give way for the present.

They all three called in Rivers Street for a couple of minutes; but

Anne convinced herself that a day’s delay of the intended communication

could be of no consequence, and hastened forward to the White Hart, to

see again the friends and companions of the last [[motifs/autumn|autumn]], with an

eagerness of good-will which many associations contributed to form.



They found Mrs Musgrove and her daughter within, and by themselves, and

Anne had the kindest welcome from each. Henrietta was exactly in that

state of recently-improved views, of fresh-formed happiness, which made

her full of regard and interest for everybody she had ever liked before


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

E che sono sempre stati ottimi amici… La piacevole prospettiva di…

Non si dovrebbe mai attenuare la luce degli altri… Dovrebbe rimanere intensa così com’è.

Uguali nella loro prosperità e comodità. Spero che vostro padre e vostra madre.

Sono piuttosto soddisfatto riguardo a entrambi.



“Oh! Sì. Mio padre sarebbe molto contento se questi signori fossero più ricchi, ”

Ma non trova altre colpe da rimproverargli… Il denaro, insomma, arriva senza problemi.

Denaro… due figlie contemporaneamente… non deve essere un’operazione molto piacevole.

E questo lo rende più rigido riguardo a molte cose… Tuttavia, non intendo dire…

“Non hanno alcun diritto su di esso. È molto appropriato che abbiano solo figlie femmine.”

Titolo:  
“Fondi comuni… e sono sicura che sia sempre stato un padre molto gentile e generoso”.

“Me… Mary non è affatto all’altezza di Henrietta. Non lo è mai stata.”

Lo conosce. Ma non gli rende giustizia, né pensa abbastanza a Winthrop.

Non riesco a farle comprendere l’importanza di quella proprietà… È davvero molto importante.

Una bella sfida, considerando i tempi attuali… E ho sempre apprezzato molto Charles Hayter.

“E non smetterò ora.”



“Genitori così eccellenti come il signor e la signora Musgrove…”, esclamò Anne.

“Dovrebbero essere felici nei matrimoni dei loro figli… Fanno di tutto per…”

Dona felicità, ne sono sicuro… Che benedizione per i giovani essere in grado di…

Che mani… Vostro padre e vostra madre sembrano davvero completamente liberi da tutto ciò…

Sentimenti ambiziosi che hanno portato a tanto comportamento scorretto e dolore.

Sia nei giovani che negli anziani. Spero che pensiate che Louisa si sia completamente ripresa.

“Ora?”



Rispose con qualche esitazione: “Sì, credo di sì… molto.”

Ripresa in sé; ma è cambiata… Non c’è più corso né salti, nulla di tutto ciò.

Ridere o ballare… sono cose completamente diverse. Se per caso si dovesse scegliere solo uno…

Con la porta un po’ chiusa a chiave, inizia a muoversi e contorcersi come una giovane gallinella…

Nell’[[motifs/water|acqua]]; e Benwick è seduto al suo gomito, leggendo versi, o forse qualcos’altro.

“Sussurrandole alle orecchie, per tutto il giorno…”



“Non può certo essere di vostro gusto…”, non poté fare a meno di ridere Anne.

“Lo so”, disse lei; “ma credo davvero che sia un giovane eccellente”.



“Senza dubbio lo è. Nessuno ne dubita; e spero che nemmeno tu pensi che io, ”

“Così illiberale da voler che ogni uomo abbia gli stessi oggetti…”

Piaceri come i miei… Ho un grande affetto per Benwick; e quando si può…

Ma fai sì che parli: ha molto da dire… La lettura, però, non gli è stata di alcun aiuto.

Danno, perché ha combattuto con la stessa bravura con cui legge. È un ragazzo coraggioso. L’ho capito.

Conoscendolo meglio di prima, l’ultima lunedì… Abbiamo avuto…

Una famosa battaglia nella caccia ai ratti per tutta la mattina nella grande casa di mio padre

Stalle. E ha interpretato il suo ruolo così [[motifs/well|benissimo]] che ho iniziato ad apprezzarlo ancora di più.

Da allora.



Qui furono interrotti dalla necessità assoluta di Charles…

Seguendo gli altri nell’ammirare specchi e porcellane… ma Anne aveva già sentito parlare di qualcos’altro.

Abbastanza per comprendere lo stato attuale di Uppercross… e gioirne

La sua felicità… E sebbene sospirasse mentre gioiva, quel sospiro non nascondeva alcuna tristezza.

Il malevolenza dell’invidia in lei… Sicuramente si sarebbe alzata contro di loro.

Se avesse potuto, avrebbe voluto benedirli, ma non voleva diminuire le loro fortune.



La visita trascorse interamente in un’atmosfera di grande allegria. Mary era.

Spirituali eccellenti, che godono della gioia e dei cambiamenti, e quindi molto [[motifs/well|bene]].

Soddisfatta del [[motifs/journey|viaggio]] fatto nella carrozza di sua suocera, con quattro cavalli.

Cavalli… e con la sua totale indipendenza rispetto a Camden Place…

Era proprio nel momento giusto per ammirare tutto come avrebbe dovuto…

Entravano facilmente in possesso di tutte le prerogative della famiglia, poiché.

Le furono spiegate nei dettagli. Non aveva alcuna richiesta da fare verso suo padre o sua sorella.

La conseguenza per lei fu semplicemente aggravata dal loro aspetto attraente…

saloni da ricevimento.



Per un breve [[motifs/time|periodo]], Elizabeth soffrì molto. Lei sentiva che.

“Si dovrebbe invitare la signora Musgrove e tutta la sua compagnia a cena da loro…”

Non riusciva a sopportare quella differenza di stile, quella riduzione…

Servitori… i quali, durante una cena, furono testimoni di ciò che accadde… persone che avevano già assistito in precedenza.

Sempre così inferiore agli Elliot di Kellynch… Era una vera lotta.

Tra la decenza e la [[concepts/vanity|vanità]]; ma fu la [[concepts/vanity|vanità]] ad avere la meglio, e poi.

“Elizabeth era di nuovo felice. Queste erano le sue ragioni interiori per esserlo: ‘Vecchio…’”

Concetti preconcebuti; ospitalità rurale; non ci proponiamo di fornire…

Cene… poche persone a Bath le fanno; Lady Alicia mai; nemmeno una volta.

Chiedi alla famiglia di sua sorella, anche se sono stati qui per un mese… E oserei dire che…

Direbbe che sarebbe molto scomodo per la signora Musgrove… La metterebbe davvero in difficoltà.

“Per la sua strada… Sono sicura che preferirebbe non venire; non si sente a suo agio in questa situazione.”

“Us… Chiederò loro tutti di trascorrere una serata con me; sarà molto meglio così.”

Titolo:  
Sarà una novità e un vero piacere… Non hanno mai visto due disegni del genere prima d’ora.

Le stanze saranno pronte entro domani sera… Saranno felici di venire.

“Sarà una festa tranquilla, piccola, ma molto elegante… E questo ci bastava.”

Elizabeth: e quando l’invito fu rivolto alle due persone presenti…

“Promessa a chi era assente, Mary ne fu completamente soddisfatta.”

Viene chiesto esplicitamente di incontrare il signor Elliot e di essere presentati alla signora…

Dalrymple e Miss Carteret, che fortunatamente erano già fidanzati

“Come… E non avrebbe potuto ricevere un’attenzione più lusinghiera. Signorina…”

Era previsto che Elliot avesse l'onore di fare visita alla signora Musgrove durante quel periodo.

All’alba; e Anne se ne andò con Charles e Mary…

Vederla direttamente insieme a Henrietta.



Il suo piano di trascorrere del tempo con [[characters/lady-russell|Lady Russell]] deve essere posticipato per il momento.

Tutti e tre rimasero al telefono per un paio di minuti in River Street; ma…

Anne si convinse che un ritardo di un giorno nella comunicazione prevista fosse accettabile.

Potrebbe non avere alcuna importanza… e si affrettò verso il White Hart.

Rivedere ancora gli amici e i compagni dell'ultimo [[motifs/autumn|autunno]], con un.

La fretta e la buona volontà con cui molte associazioni hanno contribuito a crearla.



Trovarono la signora Musgrove e sua figlia all’interno, e da sole.

Titolo:  
Anne ricevette un’accoglienza davvero calorosa da parte di tutti. Henrietta era proprio come…

Titolo:  
Lo stato di quelle visioni recentemente migliorate, di quella felicità appena nata… che rendevano tutto possibile.

Colma di attenzione e interesse per tutte le persone che aveva sempre amato in passato



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_22--part_04" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 22 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 22" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/love,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/history,concept/hope,form/history,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


at all; and Mrs Musgrove’s real affection had been won by her

usefulness when they were in distress. It was a heartiness, and a

warmth, and a sincerity which Anne delighted in the more, from the sad

want of such blessings at [[motifs/home|home]]. She was entreated to give them as much

of her [[motifs/time|time]] as possible, invited for every day and all day long, or

rather claimed as part of the family; and, in return, she naturally

fell into all her wonted ways of attention and assistance, and on

Charles’s leaving them together, was listening to Mrs Musgrove’s

[[concepts/history|history]] of Louisa, and to Henrietta’s of herself, giving opinions on

business, and recommendations to shops; with intervals of every help

which Mary required, from altering her ribbon to settling her accounts;

from finding her keys, and assorting her trinkets, to trying to

convince her that she was not ill-used by anybody; which Mary, [[motifs/well|well]]

amused as she generally was, in her station at a [[motifs/window|window]] overlooking the

entrance to the Pump Room, could not but have her moments of imagining.



A morning of thorough confusion was to be expected. A large party in an

hotel ensured a quick-changing, unsettled scene. One five minutes

brought a note, the next a parcel; and Anne had not been there half an

hour, when their dining-room, spacious as it was, seemed more than half

filled: a party of steady old friends were seated around Mrs Musgrove,

and Charles came back with Captains Harville and Wentworth. The

appearance of the latter could not be more than the surprise of the

moment. It was impossible for her to have forgotten to feel that this

arrival of their common friends must be soon bringing them together

again. Their last meeting had been most important in opening his

feelings; she had derived from it a delightful conviction; but she

feared from his looks, that the same unfortunate persuasion, which had

hastened him away from the Concert Room, still governed. He did not

seem to want to be near enough for conversation.



She tried to be calm, and leave things to take their course, and tried

to dwell much on this argument of rational dependence:—“Surely, if

there be constant attachment on each side, our hearts must understand

each other ere long. We are not boy and girl, to be captiously

irritable, misled by every moment’s inadvertence, and wantonly playing

with our own happiness.” And yet, a few minutes afterwards, she felt as

if their being in company with each other, under their present

circumstances, could only be exposing them to inadvertencies and

misconstructions of the most mischievous kind.



“Anne,” cried Mary, still at her [[motifs/window|window]], “there is Mrs Clay, I am sure,

standing under the colonnade, and a gentleman with her. I saw them turn

the corner from Bath Street just now. They seemed deep in talk. Who is

it? Come, and tell me. Good heavens! I recollect. It is Mr Elliot

himself.”



“No,” cried Anne, quickly, “it cannot be Mr Elliot, I assure you. He

was to leave Bath at nine this morning, and does not come back till

to-morrow.”



As she spoke, she felt that [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] was looking at her, the

consciousness of which vexed and embarrassed her, and made her regret

that she had said so much, simple as it was.



Mary, resenting that she should be supposed not to know her own cousin,

began talking very warmly about the family features, and protesting

still more positively that it was Mr Elliot, calling again upon Anne to

come and look for herself, but Anne did not mean to stir, and tried to

be cool and unconcerned. Her distress returned, however, on perceiving

smiles and intelligent glances pass between two or three of the lady

visitors, as if they believed themselves quite in the secret. It was

evident that the report concerning her had spread, and a short pause

succeeded, which seemed to ensure that it would now spread farther.



“Do come, Anne,” cried Mary, “come and look yourself. You will be too

late if you do not make haste. They are parting; they are shaking

hands. He is turning away. Not know Mr Elliot, indeed! You seem to have

forgot all about Lyme.”



To pacify Mary, and perhaps screen her own embarrassment, Anne did move

quietly to the [[motifs/window|window]]. She was just in [[motifs/time|time]] to ascertain that it really

was Mr Elliot, which she had never believed, before he disappeared on

one side, as Mrs Clay walked quickly off on the other; and checking the

surprise which she could not but feel at such an appearance of friendly

conference between two persons of totally opposite interest, she calmly

said, “Yes, it is Mr Elliot, certainly. He has changed his hour of

going, I suppose, that is all, or I may be mistaken, I might not

attend;” and walked back to her chair, recomposed, and with the

comfortable [[concepts/hope|hope]] of having acquitted herself [[motifs/well|well]].



The visitors took their leave; and Charles, having civilly seen them

off, and then made a face at them, and abused them for coming, began

with—



“[[motifs/well|Well]], mother, I have done something for you that you will like. I have

been to the theatre, and secured a box for to-morrow [[motifs/night|night]]. A’n’t I a

good boy? I know you [[motifs/love|love]] a play; and there is room for us all. It

holds nine. I have engaged [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]. Anne will not be sorry to

join us, I am sure. We all like a play. Have not I done [[motifs/well|well]], mother?”



Mrs Musgrove was good humouredly beginning to express her perfect

readiness for the play, if Henrietta and all the others liked it, when

Mary eagerly interrupted her by exclaiming—



“Good heavens, Charles! how can you think of such a thing? Take a box

for to-morrow [[motifs/night|night]]! Have you forgot that we are engaged to Camden

Place to-morrow [[motifs/night|night]]? and that we were most particularly asked to meet

Lady Dalrymple and her daughter, and Mr Elliot, and all the principal

family connexions, on purpose to be introduced to them? How can you be


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Assolutamente no; e l’affetto vero e proprio di Mrs Musgrove era stato conquistato da lei…

La utilità nel momento del bisogno. Era una forma di generosità e solidarietà…

Calore e sincerità: qualcosa che Anne apprezzava ancora di più… soprattutto nella tristezza.

Mancando tali benedizioni a [[motifs/home|casa]], le fu chiesto di concederle in abbondanza.

Nel modo più possibile, durante il suo [[motifs/time|tempo]], veniva invitata ogni giorno, per l’intera giornata, o qualcosa del genere.

Piuttosto considerata parte della famiglia; e, in cambio, lei naturalmente…

Si dedicò nuovamente alle sue abituali attenzioni e aiuto verso gli altri, e così fece…

“Charles li lascia insieme mentre ascolta la signora Musgrove…”

La [[concepts/history|storia]] di Louisa, e quella di Henrietta riguardo a se stessa, con opinioni al riguardo.

Consigli per gli affari e raccomandazioni ai negozi; con suggerimenti utili in ogni situazione

“Che cosa richiedesse Mary, dal modificare la sua fascia fino a sistemare i suoi conti…”

Da trovare le sue chiavi e sistemare i suoi gingillini, fino a provare…

Convincila che nessuno l’ha trattata male; cosa che Mary, [[motifs/well|benissimo]], riuscì a fare.

Come al solito divertita, nella sua posizione dietro la [[motifs/window|finestra]] che si affacciava sul.

L’ingresso alla Pump Room le provocava inevitabilmente momenti di immaginazione.



Una mattina di totale confusione era davvero da aspettarsi… Una grande festa, insomma…

L’hotel creava una scena di continua agitazione e cambiamento… ogni cinque minuti.

Portò una nota, poi un pacco; e Anne non era ancora arrivata da nemmeno mezz’ora…

Ore in cui la loro sala da pranzo, per quanto spaziosa fosse, sembrava occupata per più della metà…

Titolo:  
Riuniti intorno alla signora Musgrove, un gruppo di vecchi amici fedeli…

E Charles tornò insieme ai capitani Harville e Wentworth.

La comparsa di quest’ultimo non poteva che essere una sorpresa per tutti.

Momento… Era impossibile che lei avesse dimenticato di provare quella sensazione.

L'arrivo dei loro amici in comune li riunirà presto.

Di nuovo… Il loro ultimo incontro era stato estremamente importante per aprire nuove possibilità per lui.

Sentimenti… Ne aveva tratto una convinzione deliziosa… ma lei…

Temevano, a giudicare dal suo aspetto, che lo stesso sfortunato convincimento che aveva.

“Lo affrettarono ad allontanarsi dalla sala da concerto, ancora sotto il loro controllo… Lui non fece nulla.”

Sembra voler essere abbastanza vicino da poter conversare.



Cercò di mantenere la calma e di lasciare che le cose seguissero il loro corso…

Riflessioni sulla dipendenza razionale: “Certamente, se…”

Un legame costante da entrambe le parti: i nostri cuori devono comprenderlo

“Tra poco ci ameremo l’uno con l’altro… Non siamo più bambini, per giocare a questi scherzi.”

Irritabile, ingannato da ogni piccola negligenza del momento, e che agisce in modo capriccioso…

“Con la nostra stessa felicità…”. Eppure, pochi minuti dopo, si sentì come…

Se sono insieme, nella loro attuale situazione…

In tali circostanze, l’unica cosa che si poteva fare era esporli a infortuni o incidenti involontari…

Distorsioni del genere più malizioso possibile.



“Anne,” gridò Mary, ancora davanti alla sua [[motifs/window|finestra]], “quella è sicuramente la signora Clay, ”

Dietro la colonna, un gentiluomo con lei… Li vidi girare.

“L’angolo vicino a Bath Street… Sembravano immersi in una conversazione intima. Chi sarà?”

“Ah… Vieni pure e dimmelo. Mio Dio! Ora ricordo: è il signor Elliot.”

“Se stesso.”



“No“, esclamò Anne in fretta, “non può essere il signor Elliot, ve lo assicuro. Lui…“

Titolo:  
Avrebbe dovuto lasciare Bath alle nove di questa mattina e non tornerà fino a…

“Domani.”



Mentre parlava, sentiva che [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]] la stesse guardando.

Consapevolezza di cui si sentiva angosciata e imbarazzata, e che la faceva pentire…

Il fatto che avesse detto così tanto, anche se in modo semplice.



Mary, risentita dal fatto che si debba pensare che non conosca sua cugina…

Iniziò a parlare con grande calore delle caratteristiche familiari, protestando…

In modo ancora più deciso, fu il signor Elliot a chiamare di nuovo Anne…

“Vieni a cercarmi da sola…”, ma Anne non voleva disturbare nessuno e provò a…

Titolo:  
“Mostrarsi calmi e indifferenti… Ma la sua angoscia tornò non appena se ne rese conto.”

Sorrisi e sguardi intelligenti si scambiano tra due o tre di quelle signore

Visitatori, come se credessero di conoscere quel segreto alla perfezione…

È evidente che la notizia relativa a lei si sia diffusa, e ci fu una breve pausa…

Riuscì nel suo intento, il che sembrava garantire che la situazione si sarebbe diffusa ulteriormente.



“Vieni pure, Anne,” gridò Mary, “vieni a vedere con i tuoi occhi. Sarai sicuramente sorpresa…”

In ritardo se non ti affretti… Stanno per separarsi; si stanno salutando.

Mani… Si sta allontanando… Non conosce davvero il signor Elliot, vero? Sembra che…

“Dimenticato completamente di Lyme…”



Per placare Mary e forse anche per nascondere la propria imbarazzo, Anne decise davvero di muoversi.

Silenziosamente, si avvicinò alla [[motifs/window|finestra]]. Arrivò giusto in tempo per constatare che.

Il nome era il signor Elliot… qualcosa che lei non aveva mai creduto, prima che lui scomparisse.

Da un lato, la signora Clay se ne andava rapidamente; dall’altro… si controllava.

Una sorpresa che non poté fare a meno di provare di fronte a una tale dimostrazione di cordialità

Conferenza tra due persone con interessi totalmente opposti… lei rimane calma.

Disse: “Sì, è sicuramente il signor Elliot. Ha cambiato l’ora del suo appuntamento…”

Forse è tutto, o forse mi sbaglio…

“Attendete…” e tornò alla sua sedia, riprendendosi completamente, e con…

Una confortevole [[concepts/hope|>speranza]] di essersi comportata bene.



I visitatori se ne andarono; e Charles, dopo averli congedati in modo cortese…

“Via, e poi fece una faccia disgustata verso di loro, insultandoli per essere venuti…”

Con –



“Beh, mamma, ho fatto qualcosa per te che ti piacerà. Ho, ”

Sono stato al teatro e ho prenotato un palco per domani sera. Non sono forse.

Bambino bravo. So che ti piace molto giocare, e c’è spazio per tutti noi.

Ne contiene nove. Ho assunto [[characters/captain-wentworth|Capitano Wentworth]]. Anne non se ne pentirà.

Vieni con noi, ne sono sicuro. A tutti piace il teatro. Non ho forse fatto bene, madre?



La signora Musgrove, di buon umore, iniziava a esprimere le sue idee perfette…

Prontezza per la rappresentazione… se a Henrietta e agli altri piacerà, quando…

“Mary la interruppe con impazienza, esclamando…”



“Mio Dio, Charles! Come puoi anche solo pensare a una cosa del genere? Prendi una scatola…”

Per la prossima [[motifs/night|notte]]! Hai dimenticato che siamo fidanzati con Camden?

Dove domani sera? E ci è stato chiesto esplicitamente di incontrarci lì.

Lady Dalrymple e sua figlia, il signor Elliot… e tutti gli altri protagonisti principali

Legami familiari: per quale motivo essere presentati proprio a loro? Come è possibile…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_22--part_05" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 22 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 22" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/home,motif/silence,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/freedom,concept/imagination,concept/truth,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


so forgetful?”



“Phoo! phoo!” replied Charles, “what’s an evening party? Never worth

remembering. Your father might have asked us to dinner, I think, if he

had wanted to see us. You may do as you like, but I shall go to the

play.”



“Oh! Charles, I declare it will be too abominable if you do, when you

promised to go.”



“No, I did not promise. I only smirked and bowed, and said the word

‘happy.’ There was no promise.”



“But you must go, Charles. It would be unpardonable to fail. We were

asked on purpose to be introduced. There was always such a great

connexion between the Dalrymples and ourselves. Nothing ever happened

on either side that was not announced immediately. We are quite near

relations, you know; and Mr Elliot too, whom you ought so particularly

to be acquainted with! Every attention is due to Mr Elliot. Consider,

my father’s heir: the future representative of the family.”



“Don’t talk to me about heirs and representatives,” cried Charles. “I

am not one of those who neglect the reigning power to bow to the rising

sun. If I would not go for the sake of your father, I should think it

scandalous to go for the sake of his heir. What is Mr Elliot to me?”

The careless expression was life to Anne, who saw that Captain

Wentworth was all attention, looking and listening with his whole [[motifs/soul|soul]];

and that the last words brought his enquiring eyes from Charles to

herself.



Charles and Mary still talked on in the same style; he, half serious

and half jesting, maintaining the scheme for the play, and she,

invariably serious, most warmly opposing it, and not omitting to make

it known that, however determined to go to Camden Place herself, she

should not think herself very [[motifs/well|well]] used, if they went to the play

without her. Mrs Musgrove interposed.



“We had better put it off. Charles, you had much better go back and

change the box for Tuesday. It would be a pity to be divided, and we

should be losing Miss Anne, too, if there is a party at her father’s;

and I am sure neither Henrietta nor I should care at all for the play,

if Miss Anne could not be with us.”



Anne felt truly obliged to her for such kindness; and quite as much so

for the opportunity it gave her of decidedly saying—



“If it depended only on my inclination, ma’am, the party at [[motifs/home|home]]

(excepting on Mary’s account) would not be the smallest impediment. I

have no pleasure in the sort of meeting, and should be too happy to

change it for a play, and with you. But, it had better not be

attempted, perhaps.” She had spoken it; but she trembled when it was

done, conscious that her words were listened to, and daring not even to

try to observe their effect.



It was soon generally agreed that Tuesday should be the day; Charles

only reserving the advantage of still teasing his wife, by persisting

that he would go to the play to-morrow if nobody else would.



[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] left his seat, and walked to the [[motifs/fire|fire]]-place; probably

for the sake of walking away from it soon afterwards, and taking a

station, with less bare-faced design, by Anne.



“You have not been long enough in Bath,” said he, “to enjoy the evening

parties of the place.”



“Oh! no. The usual character of them has nothing for me. I am no

card-player.”



“You were not formerly, I know. You did not use to like cards; but [[motifs/time|time]]

makes many changes.”



“I am not yet so much changed,” cried Anne, and stopped, fearing she

hardly knew what misconstruction. After waiting a few moments he said,

and as if it were the result of immediate feeling, “It is a period,

indeed! Eight years and a half is a period.”



Whether he would have proceeded farther was left to Anne’s [[concepts/imagination|imagination]]

to ponder over in a calmer hour; for while still hearing the sounds he

had uttered, she was startled to other subjects by Henrietta, eager to

make use of the present leisure for getting out, and calling on her

companions to lose no [[motifs/time|time]], lest somebody else should come in.



They were obliged to move. Anne talked of being perfectly ready, and

tried to look it; but she felt that could Henrietta have known the

regret and reluctance of her heart in quitting that chair, in preparing

to quit the room, she would have found, in all her own sensations for

her cousin, in the very security of his affection, wherewith to pity

her.



Their preparations, however, were stopped short. Alarming sounds were

heard; other visitors approached, and the door was thrown open for Sir

Walter and Miss Elliot, whose entrance seemed to give a general chill.

Anne felt an instant oppression, and wherever she looked saw symptoms

of the same. The comfort, the [[concepts/freedom|freedom]], the gaiety of the room was over,

hushed into cold composure, determined [[motifs/silence|silence]], or insipid talk, to

meet the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How mortifying to

feel that it was so!



Her jealous eye was satisfied in one particular. [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] was

acknowledged again by each, by Elizabeth more graciously than before.

She even addressed him once, and looked at him more than once.

Elizabeth was, in fact, revolving a great measure. The sequel explained

it. After the waste of a few minutes in saying the proper nothings, she

began to give the invitation which was to comprise all the remaining

dues of the Musgroves. “To-morrow evening, to meet a few friends: no

formal party.” It was all said very gracefully, and the cards with

which she had provided herself, the “Miss Elliot at [[motifs/home|home]],” were laid on

the table, with a courteous, comprehensive smile to all, and one smile

Elizabeth arose and disappeared.



The interruption had been short, though severe, and ease and animation

returned to most of those they left as the door shut them out, but not

to Anne. She could think only of the invitation she had with such

astonishment witnessed, and of the manner in which it had been

received; a manner of doubtful meaning, of surprise rather than

gratification, of polite acknowledgement rather than acceptance. She

knew him; she saw disdain in his eye, and could not venture to believe

that he had determined to accept such an offering, as an atonement for

all the insolence of the past. Her spirits sank. He held the card in

his hand after they were gone, as if deeply considering it.



“Only think of Elizabeth’s including everybody!” whispered Mary very

audibly. “I do not [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] is delighted! You see he

cannot put the card out of his hand.”



Anne caught his eye, saw his cheeks glow, and his mouth form itself

into a momentary expression of contempt, and turned away, that she

might neither see nor hear more to vex her.



The party separated. The gentlemen had their own pursuits, the ladies

proceeded on their own business, and they met no more while Anne

belonged to them. She was earnestly begged to return and dine, and give

them all the rest of the day, but her spirits had been so long exerted

that at present she felt unequal to more, and fit only for [[motifs/home|home]], where

she might be sure of being as silent as she chose.



Promising to be with them the whole of the following morning,

therefore, she closed the fatigues of the present by a toilsome walk to

Camden Place, there to spend the evening chiefly in listening to the

busy arrangements of Elizabeth and Mrs Clay for the morrow’s party, the

frequent enumeration of the persons invited, and the continually

improving detail of all the embellishments which were to make it the

most completely elegant of its kind in Bath, while harassing herself

with the never-ending question, of whether [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]] would come

or not? They were reckoning him as certain, but with her it was a

gnawing solicitude never appeased for five minutes together. She

generally thought he would come, because she generally thought he

ought; but it was a case which she could not so shape into any positive

act of duty or discretion, as inevitably to defy the suggestions of

very opposite feelings.



She only roused herself from the broodings of this restless agitation,

to let Mrs Clay know that she had been seen with Mr Elliot three hours

after his being supposed to be out of Bath, for having watched in vain

for some intimation of the interview from the lady herself, she

determined to mention it, and it seemed to her there was [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] in Mrs

Clay’s face as she listened. It was transient: cleared away in an

instant; but Anne could imagine she read there the consciousness of

having, by some complication of mutual trick, or some overbearing

authority of his, been obliged to attend (perhaps for half an hour) to

his lectures and restrictions on her designs on Sir Walter. She

exclaimed, however, with a very tolerable imitation of [[concepts/nature|nature]]:—



“Oh! dear! very true. Only think, Miss Elliot, to my great surprise I

met with Mr Elliot in Bath Street. I was never more astonished. He

turned back and walked with me to the Pump Yard. He had been prevented

setting off for Thornberry, but I really forget by what; for I was in a

hurry, and could not much attend, and I can only answer for his being

determined not to be delayed in his return. He wanted to know how early

he might be admitted to-morrow. He was full of ‘to-morrow,’ and it is

very evident that I have been full of it too, ever since I entered the

house, and learnt the extension of your plan and all that had happened,

or my seeing him could never have gone so entirely out of my head.”

>Casa, e venne a sapere dell’estensione del tuo piano e di tutto ciò che era accaduto.

“O forse il mio ricordo di lui non avrebbe mai potuto svanire del tutto dalla mia mente.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_23--part_01" data-title="Persuasion — Chapter 23 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 23" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/faith,concept/history,concept/self,concept/truth,form/history,character/captain_wentworth"></span>


CHAPTER XXIII.





One day only had passed since Anne’s conversation with Mrs Smith; but a

keener interest had succeeded, and she was now so little touched by Mr

Elliot’s conduct, except by its effects in one quarter, that it became

a matter of course the next morning, still to defer her explanatory

visit in Rivers Street. She had promised to be with the Musgroves from

breakfast to dinner. Her [[concepts/faith|faith]] was plighted, and Mr Elliot’s character,

like the Sultaness Scheherazade’s head, must live another day.



She could not keep her appointment punctually, however; the weather was

unfavourable, and she had grieved over the rain on her friends’

account, and felt it very much on her own, before she was able to

attempt the walk. When she reached the White Hart, and made her way to

the proper apartment, she found herself neither arriving quite in [[motifs/time|time]],

nor the first to arrive. The party before her were, Mrs Musgrove,

talking to Mrs Croft, and Captain Harville to [[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]; and

she immediately heard that Mary and Henrietta, too impatient to wait,

had gone out the moment it had cleared, but would be back again soon,

and that the strictest injunctions had been left with Mrs Musgrove to

keep her there till they returned. She had only to submit, sit down, be

outwardly composed, and feel herself plunged at once in all the

agitations which she had merely laid her account of tasting a little

before the morning closed. There was no delay, no waste of [[motifs/time|time]]. She

was deep in the happiness of such misery, or the misery of such

happiness, instantly. Two minutes after her entering the room, Captain

Wentworth said—



“We will write the letter we were talking of, Harville, now, if you

will give me materials.”



Materials were at hand, on a separate table; he went to it, and nearly

turning his back to them all, was engrossed by writing.



Mrs Musgrove was giving Mrs Croft the [[concepts/history|history]] of her eldest daughter’s

engagement, and just in that inconvenient tone of voice which was

perfectly audible while it pretended to be a whisper. Anne felt that

she did not belong to the conversation, and yet, as Captain Harville

seemed thoughtful and not disposed to talk, she could not avoid hearing

many undesirable particulars; such as, “how Mr Musgrove and my brother

Hayter had met again and again to talk it over; what my brother Hayter

had said one day, and what Mr Musgrove had proposed the next, and what

had occurred to my sister Hayter, and what the young people had wished,

and what I said at first I never could consent to, but was afterwards

persuaded to think might do very [[motifs/well|well]],” and a great deal in the same

style of open-hearted communication: minutiae which, even with every

advantage of taste and delicacy, which good Mrs Musgrove could not

give, could be properly interesting only to the principals. Mrs Croft

was attending with great good-humour, and whenever she spoke at all, it

was very sensibly. Anne hoped the gentlemen might each be too much

[[concepts/self|self]]-occupied to hear.



“And so, ma’am, all these thing considered,” said Mrs Musgrove, in her

powerful whisper, “though we could have wished it different, yet,

altogether, we did not think it fair to stand out any longer, for

Charles Hayter was quite wild about it, and Henrietta was pretty near

as bad; and so we thought they had better marry at once, and make the

best of it, as many others have done before them. At any rate, said I,

it will be better than a long engagement.”



“That is precisely what I was going to observe,” cried Mrs Croft. “I

would rather have young people settle on a small income at once, and

have to struggle with a few difficulties together, than be involved in

a long engagement. I always think that no mutual—”



“Oh! dear Mrs Croft,” cried Mrs Musgrove, unable to let her finish her

speech, “there is nothing I so abominate for young people as a long

engagement. It is what I always protested against for my children. It

is all very [[motifs/well|well]], I used to say, for young people to be engaged, if

there is a certainty of their being able to marry in six months, or

even in twelve; but a long engagement—”



“Yes, dear ma’am,” said Mrs Croft, “or an uncertain engagement, an

engagement which may be long. To begin without knowing that at such a

[[motifs/time|time]] there will be the means of marrying, I hold to be very unsafe and

unwise, and what I think all parents should prevent as far as they

can.”



Anne found an unexpected interest here. She felt its application to

herself, felt it in a nervous thrill all over her; and at the same

moment that her eyes instinctively glanced towards the distant table,

[[characters/captain-wentworth|Captain Wentworth]]’s pen ceased to move, his head was raised, pausing,

listening, and he turned round the next instant to give a look, one

quick, conscious look at her.



The two ladies continued to talk, to re-urge the same admitted truths,

and enforce them with such examples of the ill effect of a contrary

practice as had fallen within their observation, but Anne heard nothing

distinctly; it was only a buzz of words in her ear, her mind was in

confusion.



Captain Harville, who had in [[concepts/truth|truth]] been hearing none of it, now left

his seat, and moved to a [[motifs/window|window]], and Anne seeming to watch him, though

it was from thorough absence of mind, became gradually sensible that he

was inviting her to join him where he stood. He looked at her with a

smile, and a little motion of the head, which expressed, “Come to me, I

have something to say;” and the unaffected, easy kindness of manner

which denoted the feelings of an older acquaintance than he really was,

strongly enforced the invitation. She roused herself and went to him.

The [[motifs/window|window]] at which he stood was at the other end of the room from

where the two ladies were sitting, and though nearer to Captain

Wentworth’s table, not very near. As she joined him, Captain Harville’s
